headline: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
body:
Trump says he won't allow American companies to build data centres "outside" the US

Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.

"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.

Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.

"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.

"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."

But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.

"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.

Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.

Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.

It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.

Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.

The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.

Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back

Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.

As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.

Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.

"You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.

"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."

Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.

Meta has already broken ground on a data centre, external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.

The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.

In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.

Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.

Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".

Google has been contacted for comment.

This was the first COP since the UN warned that global temperatures are expected to exceed 1.5C degrees above pre-industrial levels. That is the threshold which countries agreed not to breach as part of the Paris Climate Agreement signed in 2015.

The draft agreement had acknowledged the uncomfortable reality that climate action to date has failed on its most crucial of targets.

Without agreement, that recognition has been lost.

Almost exactly a decade ago a group of the world's climate scientists - the official UN body the IPCC - warned what would happen if temperatures rose 1.5C vs 2C:

Sea level rise would be 10cm higher - that would expose 10 million more people to flooding, external

The ocean would become more acidic risking irreversible damage to some marine life

Extreme heat - that's hot days and nights - in every inhabited part of the world

In a 2C world extreme heat is expected to be experienced in every inhabitated area on Earth

Throughout the talks and during the final day, many countries still acknowledged that the target remained their north star of climate action.

"This COP sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with even more urgency to reduce emissions," said UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh at the close of the talks.

The draft had called for that overshoot to be kept as small and short-lived as possible – it also suggested something called carbon dioxide removal (CDR).

This is a process which takes greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere and has not been explicitly mentioned in a COP final agreement before.

Carbon dioxide can be removed naturally by planting trees - although there are limits to the scale and permanence of that.

There are other technological solutions, but these are controversial, external and are not well advanced.

This year's negotiations have exposed a troubling problem - consensus does not last forever.

On the central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts – countries could not bridge the divide on including language on fossil fuels.

And yet the very same pledge had been made just three years ago at COP28 in Dubai.

Rich nations also failed to put a figure to how much more money could be given to developing countries to adapt to climate change.

This is despite there already being a commitment from last year to triple the figure by 2035 from $40bn (£30bn) - but the interpretation of that pledge remains contested.

If governments cannot even agree to reaffirm commitments they've already made, it raises troubling questions about their ability to work together as the climate crisis intensifies.

Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed

Minister Chris Bowen from Australia, who was co-leading the negotiations, pointed out at the end of the talks that the world is a very different place from when these commitments were struck just a few years ago.

"The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory".

That was made apparent during the final meeting when pointed remarks were delivered. EU representative Darragh O'Brien said the talks had been "hijacked by some oil states".

Russian delegate Sergei Kononuchenko switched from Russian to English to directly address the EU delegation. He accused them of providing climate finance only in the form of loans to developing nations: "This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner".

It is a serious blow not just to climate action, but to multilateralism itself - the idea that countries can put aside their differences on other issues to tackle problems they can't solve alone.

Much of the coverage of COP31 has focused on the failure to get the central political agreement passed.

But much of the work at these summits is putting into action agreements made at previous meetings.

On money that is going towards adaptation for example, countries need to agree how is it being distributed, is it making an impact and how can this be tracked, and which areas are particularly vulnerable.

In fact, there were 164 other items on this year's agenda that were being thrashed out in the negotiating rooms.

And some of those were agreed at the talks.

The funds raised from a global system of carbon credits – money given in exchange for releasing greenhouse gases – will go towards helping developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change.

They agreed to advance a just transition framework designed to protect workers and communities as global economies shift toward clean energy.

But there were many more that could not be agreed and some will now be picked up at COP32, including crucially the work programme responsible for driving forward action on cutting emissions.

What governments agree in the COP negotiating rooms is only part of what determines the speed of the energy transition.

The International Energy Agency's latest World Energy Outlook, external points to another powerful force: energy security.

It says the disruption to oil and gas supplies through the Strait of Hormuz has been the biggest energy supply shock in history. The longer the uncertainty continues, the stronger the incentive for countries to switch from imported fossil fuels to electricity generated at home.

Renewable energy capacity is expected to grow 60% more over the next six-year period than the previous

The economics have been changing too.

Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles have become increasingly competitive.

As clean energy develops its own commercial momentum, formal negotiations may become less important in determining its direction and pace.

Against the headwinds of inflation new investment announcements emerged at COP as part of the "Action Agenda".

This is the part of the COP process that tries to mobilise action outside of formal talks from businesses, investors and cities – this year the focus was on electrification. Turning more of our energy from fossil fuels to electricity.

"We are not entering the age of electricity, we have arrived at the age of electricity," Fatih Birol, head of the IEA, told the BBC. He says energy security and climate policies are now "closely aligned".

That doesn't make COP irrelevant.

Governments still have a crucial role in facilitating the transition, according to Dr Jennie Dodson, a senior director at the World Business Council for Sustainable Development which includes among its members the likes of Amazon and Apple.

"A key message from business is we can go so far, a lot of it is cost competitive, but there are policy barriers both around infrastructure and permitting".

Many are questioning whether the COP process is fit for purpose

COP31 has shown how the role of these annual UN climate conferences is changing.

For the first 30 COPs, the emphasis was on building the international framework for tackling global warming.

The great diplomatic breakthrough came in Paris in 2015, when almost every country agreed to keep global warming well below 2°C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.

Paris also established machinery designed to turn promises into progress. Every five years, governments assess collective progress in a global stocktake and submit new national climate plans, known as NDCs.

Then came further agreements: a fund for climate damage at COP27, a commitment to transition away from fossil fuels and triple renewable energy capacity at COP28, a new climate finance target at COP29 and increased support for adaptation at COP30.

The international architecture for tackling climate change has, in other words, largely been built.

Now comes the harder business of making it work. That's why this year's conference in Antalya, Turkey, had been billed as an "implementation COP".

The emphasis now is shifting towards delivering commitments already made. Camilla Born, who helped develop the UK's strategy for COP26 and now heads the campaign group Electrify Britain, told the BBC this is making COP more procedural - less about fundamental negotiations than ensuring the machinery actually works.

This could mean doing away with a cover text – the central political agreement that countries sign up to with new pledges.

It is not a requirement to have one, and for many years countries managed without. Australia chose to push one for this COP, and it is where they fell down.

On many of the procedural issues Camilla Bonn spoke of, they did agree things. That may be important. It isn't necessarily exciting.

And there is a fundamental limit to what this machinery can achieve. Under the Paris Agreement countries have no mechanism to force them to meet their emissions targets.

So, when critics berate the COP process for failing to tackle the problem fast enough, it isn't really the system that is at fault, says Alden Meyer, a veteran climate negotiator now at the climate think tank E3G.

The COP process, he suggests, is "like a mirror that we hold up to ourselves every year". If the reflection is disappointing, the problem is the governments, not the mirror.

Hours after Friday's strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".

Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.

However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".

"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he told CNN.

Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he was a "friend" meant "he doesn't feel enough pressure".

The war of words came as neighbouring Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace in the south-east of the country early on Friday.

Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said the missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

This was about 100km from where European troops - from 11 of the 36 member nations of the coalition of the willing - were completing a training exercise, Polish authorities said. Another cruise missile and a jet-powered drone were suspected to have hit two other locations, they added.

On Saturday, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski told the BBC the cruise missiles had guidance systems, so "it is very unlikely that they veered off course as a result of Ukrainian electronic warfare".

"This is a war in Europe that affects our security," he told Radio 4's Today programme, also referencing similar incidents in recent months across Europe.

Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said the military alliance had scrambled its jets in response.

Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine.

Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

headline: Burnham to tell MPs 'landmark' EU deal could make next decade 'much better'
body:
Andy Burnham agreed a deal with the EU in Brussels on Friday

The prime minister will tell Parliament on Monday the "landmark" deal struck with the EU means there is a "very real prospect" the next decade can be "much better" than the last one.

The deal, which covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme, is a "choice between a broken status quo or change", Andy Burnham will tell MPs.

He will also call it "the single biggest growth measure to be delivered in this parliament" - repeating his claim it could add £17bn to the British economy.

But opposition parties have criticised the plan, with the Conservatives branding it unfair as UK farmers would have to follow rules made by Brussels.

The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.

Meanwhile, the new youth experience scheme, which is due to launch no later than January 2030, will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31-year-olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.

Burnham believes the agreement reached in Brussels "holds out the very real prospect that the next decade can be a much better one for Britain than the one we have just lived through".

"The ability to draw a line on a decade of drift and division is in our hands and I believe we should take it," he will say in his speech.

He will also paint the move as a choice "between easing pressure on the cost of living or allowing food prices to rise further" and "creating opportunities for young people or denying them".

He believes polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch will use a speech at the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) annual conference on Monday to criticise Burnham's EU deal.

She will argue the prime minister should be "aiming a lot higher" on driving economic growth.

"Of course, Europe will always remain an important market. but it is not the market of the future," she will say.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage will tell the same conference that establishing closer ties with the EU would be a "disaster" for British businesses that are trying to compete and innovate.

Tories would scrap Burnham's deal with EU, deputy leader says

'Move on!' Former PMs pile in with advice for Andy Burnham, but will he listen?

On Friday, the PM said that over the coming months both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at the options for the UK's "long-term relationship" with the EU.

He was clear that the deal he struck was "probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it".

He added: "But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."

Burnham has previously suggested potential options for the future could include rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.

However, he has ruled out major changes to the UK-EU relationship before the next general election, saying he will stick to Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.

A number of former prime ministers have warned against reopening the debate over rejoining the EU.

Rishi Sunak told Sky News the issue was "divisive" and "ends up being a huge distraction for government".

Fellow Conservative former PM Baroness Theresa May told the BBC she was "aghast" Burnham could be considering rejoining the EU.

She urged him to "accept Brexit and move on".

Meanwhile, former Labour PM Sir Tony Blair, who was a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, told the Sunday Times Britain should only rejoin the bloc if it reforms, and allows more innovation on technology.

headline: Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
body:
Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.

His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media.

Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales.

The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".

The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.

Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.

Paolo Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.

The Bulgari family favoured bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected colour combinations to set them apart from the delicate asethetic associated with Parisian jewellery houses.

The business broke into luxury markets and diversified beyond jewellery into watches, perfumes, leather goods and hotels.

headline: Is the global far right really in retreat?
body:
Asian Studies in Africa at the University of Pretoria.

Not too long ago, we were grappling with the surge of a global far-right alliance. And in early 2025, when United States President Donald Trump returned for a second term, members of this global alliance must have felt that they were on the brink of securing a global hegemony.

Yet, less than two years in, this alliance seems to be losing its grip on power – and fast.

The first casualty was Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban, whose reign of 16 years ended earlier this year with a decisive loss in the parliamentary elections. He was somewhat of a “golden boy” of this movement, as Hungary under him had become the pinnacle of far-right state capture.

In fact, Orban was so important to the global right that he received election endorsements from the likes of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Alternative for Germany (AfD) leader Alice Weidel. Even US Vice President JD Vance showed up in Budapest five days before the elections to reiterate the Trump administration’s endorsement of Orban’s bid for a fifth consecutive term in office.

Yet, less than two years in, this alliance seems to be losing its grip on power – and fast.

The first casualty was Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban, whose reign of 16 years ended earlier this year with a decisive loss in the parliamentary elections. He was somewhat of a “golden boy” of this movement, as Hungary under him had become the pinnacle of far-right state capture.

In fact, Orban was so important to the global right that he received election endorsements from the likes of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Alternative for Germany (AfD) leader Alice Weidel. Even US Vice President JD Vance showed up in Budapest five days before the elections to reiterate the Trump administration’s endorsement of Orban’s bid for a fifth consecutive term in office.

In a tight race in late October, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva secured a fourth term after defeating far-right Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in the run-off. Notably, Lula’s challenger was the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. Bolsonaro senior is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup following his loss to Lula in the 2022 presidential election.

Netanyahu has been a central figure in the global alliance of the far right. At a time of genocidal violence and pogroms targeting Palestinians in the Gaza Strip and across the occupied West Bank, Netanyahu’s far-right friends have remained unmoved in their support of Israel.

But on October 27, neither the Netanyahu-led bloc nor any opposition alliance secured the required 61 seats in the parliamentary elections. Because opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot received the endorsement of Arab-led parties, he has now been invited by President Isaac Herzog to form the next government.

In the 2026 Serbian parliamentary elections, the Student List defeated Aleksandar Vucic’s party. This was a resounding victory for the student-led anticorruption movement that took to the streets against the populist leader after a railway station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in November 2024, killing 16 people.

Of course, the most significant challenge to the far right’s bid for global capture came in the form of the “blue wave” in the 2026 US midterm elections. On their way to victory, many Democratic candidates openly embraced progressive agendas, publicly expressed support for the Palestinian cause, criticised Israel and the role of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) in US politics and blasted their establishment predecessors for their “middle of the road” stance on issues at home and abroad.

Following a damning critique of the Trump administration, the Democratic Party is now set to control both chambers of Congress from January.

Already last year, Zohran Mamdani’s victory in New York City’s mayoral election showed that a progressive candidate could overcome opposition from both the right and the Democratic establishment. His run for office was marred by xenophobic and Islamophobic attacks coming from both Republicans and establishment Democrats.

He was also accused of anti-Semitism for his criticism of Netanyahu and his past pro-Palestine organising. Yet, it was his unrelenting focus on making New York more affordable and liveable and his refusal to back down from his criticism of Israel during an ongoing genocide that gave him the win in the end.

Despite all this, I would say the demise of the far right is not yet a done deal.

Undoubtedly, far-right leaders everywhere will closely study the recent defeats of their political allies and learn from their mistakes. They will have noticed the fragility of the cult of personality of the likes of Orban in the face of years of repression and state-sanctioned corruption. They will also learn from Trump’s militarism and misadventures in the Middle East. Proclaiming a war thousands of miles away as an existential battle for the good of humanity cannot eclipse the everyday concerns of common citizens.

Most importantly, though, they will bank on the historical failings of the left. They know that without a systematic effort to remedy the conditions that led to the rise of the far right in the first place, the establishment liberals will not be able to convert these wins into long-term gains.

It is, of course, easy to attribute the global rise of the far right to the machinations of individual leaders. The Netanyahus, Bolsonaros, Modis and the Trumps of the world are undoubtedly the mascots of this movement’s global ambitions. And so it is comforting to believe that the fall of an individual leader would bring about the demise of the political movement.

But to believe this would be to ignore the fact that their rise to power is only a symptom of wider structural malaise in politics and society. These leaders have weaponised legitimate public concerns regarding youth unemployment, the hollowing of the public sector, income inequality, neoliberalisation and “big money” in politics into fodder for repression, culture wars, militarism, racism and xenophobia.

The far right may have suffered losses at the ballot box because of its misadventures in power. But if progressives are to make significant gains, it cannot be business as usual.

Concretely, in a place like the US, this means that we have to recognise that the “blue wave” was more of an assertive vote against Trump rather than a wholehearted embrace of the Democratic Party. Progressives have ridden this wave into office, but for the progressive agenda to see the light of day, establishment Democrats need to step aside.

Here I’m thinking of the likes of Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer. Throughout Trump’s second term, they have chosen to engage in symbolic acts of opposition, including “strongly worded letters” and “colour-coordinated outfits”. They have, thus far, refrained from directly confronting the Trump administration and even fumbled a crucial vote on an attempt to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, with 11 House Democrats absent. They have also been slow to support progressive candidates’ bids for office and slower to come to the aid of fellow Democratic leaders being bullied by the Trump administration.

So, if the “blue wave” has to mean anything, such leaders need to be expunged from the mainstream for more progressive agendas to take hold.

In Hungary, Peter Magyar and his Tisza Party may have ended Orban’s reign. But we must remember that Magyar is hardly a progressive. Orbanism, as Gregoire Roos explains, hinged on “deeply rooted social preferences: a strong state, scepticism of external constraint, transactional politics, and sovereignty as a governing method”. These preferences remain a part of the “Hungarian political culture and do not vanish on election night”. More noteworthy is that Magyar subscribed to this brand of Orbanism until the 2024 presidential pardon scandal prompted his break with Orban’s Fidesz party.

Magyar has certainly made headway in dismantling some of the structures of Orbanism. But for progressives to make any significant gains, they would need to use the opening provided by the elections to alter the political culture in Hungary.

For those of us who have closely followed Israeli politics, it is difficult not to shrug at the recent election results. The vote was against Netanyahu, but not for a progressive future.

Removing Netanyahu – the architect of the genocide – would be a necessary step. But we must also remember that the erasure of Palestinians is a structural outgrowth of Zionism. This is why, in the lead-up to the recent elections, none of the leading Jewish-led opposition candidates campaigned on recognising a Palestinian state or offered a fundamental departure from Israel’s policies towards Palestinians.

The year 2026 has undoubtedly been a bad one for the global far right. But the current moment is far more critical for progressive forces than it is for the far right. How the left learns from the far right’s defeats, as well as the victories of unabashedly progressive candidates, will determine whether this year marks the beginning of the end of the global far right.

As a final flourish, the Spaniard ascended a staircase accompanied by the silhouette of a goat on the screen, a nod to his growing ‘Greatest of All Time’ status, before receiving a golden commemorative helmet from Agostini himself.

He then attached another plaque with his name engraved on it on the Tower of Champions before embracing and lifting it over his head.

Marquez’s latest triumph is even more remarkable given the Spaniard’s injury- and crash-blighted campaign in which he had to wait until the eighth race in Hungary on June 7 before claiming his first win.

Marquez suffered a flat tyre in the season-opener in Thailand in March, fell at the Spanish GP in Jerez and again at the French GP where he picked up a foot fracture which ruled him out of the following race, the Catalan GP.

Making his comeback at the Italian GP in Mugello, he trailed Bezzecchi by 102 points in early June, just weeks after undergoing foot surgery on top of a previous operation on his injured shoulder.

But the Spaniard managed to bounce back once again, defying those who had already written him off.

Once he got rolling, he roared into a regular winning run with seven Grands Prix and 10 sprint race victories in all this season.

While not as obviously dominant as winning 11 GPs in the 2025 season, when an unexpected return to form following his 2024 switch to Ducati gave him a new lease of life, the latest win is as impressive.

Marquez had been the youngest-ever premier-class champion in his debut season in 2013 for Honda and then went on to win the title in five of the next six seasons.

He also overtook his great rival Valentino Rossi, who won seven MotoGP titles, although the swashbuckling Italian has 89 individual race wins in the top category compared with Marquez’s 80.

Having crashed during Saturday’s sprint race, Marquez rode out Sunday’s GP safely, needing only to finish in the top nine to secure his 10th title across all categories combined.

Aprilia’s Bezzecchi won Sunday’s race to complete the double in Portugal, having also won the sprint, with his stablemate Jorge Martin of Spain crossing in second.

With a total of 439 points and seven victories this year, this was enough for Marquez to keep his rivals at bay.

Martin is second with 396 points but only one win, and Bezzecchi, who has 394 points and seven first-place finishes, is third ahead of the season finale in Valencia, Spain, next weekend.

“Thank you for this bike,” Marquez told his team Ducati during his victory lap.

headline: Europe’s hot autumn of protests is a symptom of economic breakdown
body:
Europe is in the grips of a “hot autumn”. For several weeks now, French students have led mass protests against underinvestment in education, teacher shortages and dilapidated classrooms.

In Spain, mass protests broke out after the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home of 70 years, after her rent was hiked by 230 percent by an investment fund that bought the property. She died a fortnight later after being admitted to hospital.

Now the protests are spreading: to Italy, where upwards of one million people took to the streets of 50 cities last week; to Portugal, where tent encampments have sprung up to oppose rapid hikes in housing costs; to Germany, where riot police with water cannon confronted protesters opposing the creeping extension of conscription; and most recently, to the United Kingdom, where thousands of students joined a day of action on November 20 under the slogan “Fight for our future, not their wars!”

The common thread which has sparked these Gen Z protests is the rapidly rising cost of living. In the wake of the global pandemic, the war in Ukraine, US tariffs, and now the US-Israel war on Iran, global supply chains are breaking down, sending costs spiralling.

Europe is in the grips of a “hot autumn”. For several weeks now, French students have led mass protests against underinvestment in education, teacher shortages and dilapidated classrooms.

In Spain, mass protests broke out after the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home of 70 years, after her rent was hiked by 230 percent by an investment fund that bought the property. She died a fortnight later after being admitted to hospital.

Now the protests are spreading: to Italy, where upwards of one million people took to the streets of 50 cities last week; to Portugal, where tent encampments have sprung up to oppose rapid hikes in housing costs; to Germany, where riot police with water cannon confronted protesters opposing the creeping extension of conscription; and most recently, to the United Kingdom, where thousands of students joined a day of action on November 20 under the slogan “Fight for our future, not their wars!”

The common thread which has sparked these Gen Z protests is the rapidly rising cost of living. In the wake of the global pandemic, the war in Ukraine, US tariffs, and now the US-Israel war on Iran, global supply chains are breaking down, sending costs spiralling.

But this is only a symptom of a wider problem. Deregulation and neoliberal policies have allowed corporations to take over not only the economy but also politics. This has led to massive wealth concentration at the top and increasing precarity for the vast majority of the European population. The impact of climate change and the rollout of artificial intelligence (AI), threatening mass unemployment, are making the situation a lot worse.

If we want to change course, we need to fundamentally rethink how our economy works. And yet we are ruled by a political class which has lost its will to govern.

Of course, our rulers still clamour for the perks of office. But they are operating within a logic which prevents them from taking the action necessary to deal with the challenges humanity faces. In this crisis, the centre cannot hold, and support for both radical right and left-wing parties is growing rapidly.

The problem is this: 40 years ago, politicians came to accept that the free market held the answer to all our problems. Governments gave up trying to manage the economy. By handing the levers of control to the private sector, they were told they would unleash the forces of competition and economic growth, free from the sclerotic hand of the state.

As the decades wore on, it became increasingly clear that the market looked less like multiple small businesses competing for customers and more like gigantic corporations forcing citizens, governments and the planet itself to bend to their will.

Power has been handed to monopolies, which have stretched supply chains to a breaking point, privatised profits while socialising costs, fuelled inequality and trashed the environment.

Key economic decisions once made by elected governments with at least a pretence of public interest in mind are today made in corporate boardrooms, with only the self-interest of their rich investors to trouble them.

When economic decisions are designed primarily to enrich the few, is it any wonder our public infrastructure is crumbling? The things we need to make life acceptable – housing, education, healthcare – have become no more than commodities from which the monopolists can profit.

Politicians are dismantling our welfare state, claiming that today we can no longer afford to care for the poorest. They have it the wrong way around. Rather, we cannot afford the rich.

In today’s crisis, some in Europe have come to accept the need for industrial strategy, for economic planning and government intervention; all tools which were abandoned at the onset of the “free market” era.

But these tools cannot be used properly without taking power back from the monopolies – fundamentally shifting the relationship between those who now own society and those of us who live in it. It requires a New Deal at least on the scale of President Franklin D Roosevelt’s policies in the 1930s in the United States.

And in some ways, our task is even bigger today. After World War II, European politicians built a new social contract: we would all share in the massive economic growth which would be unlocked as countries recovered from war and exploited the Earth as never before. With high growth, the poor could get richer even while the rich themselves did well.

In a world facing massive resource constraints, we can no longer operate in this way. Indeed, the richest countries have already used up their fair share of global resources.

One way out is to reassert Western dominance. The one economic area in which European governments will invest is the war machine. Even Germany’s steadfast commitment to balanced budgets – a commitment which it has disastrously imposed on the European Union with almost religious zeal – can seemingly be broken when the military demands it.

But military spending will not resuscitate European industry. Nor will it keep us safe. It will further empower the monopolies who soak up ever more of our taxes while bringing catastrophic conflict ever closer. This is not protecting us from invasion but protecting Europe’s ability to do what it wants, when it wants, where it wants. We cannot, any longer, build prosperity and security on injustice. The youth protests get that; just look at the explicitly antimilitary slogans on the streets of German cities.

A real solution requires a much bigger shift in thinking. We need to accept that Europe is entering a post-growth world, where society’s resources need to be fundamentally reallocated.

This change will not be easy. It needs politicians with the will and the ability to remove power from the corporations, to break up monopoly capitalism. And that will not come from above because, as American statesman Frederick Douglass said: “power concedes nothing without a demand”.

Europe’s youth demand radical change. Hope lies with them.

headline: Zelenskyy says Ukraine behind drone attacks on Russian ships near Libya
body:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukrainian forces sank ⁠a Russian warship off the coast of Libya, hailing an “exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war”.

Zelenskyy said in a statement on Monday that Ukrainian forces also hit a Russian dry ⁠cargo ship, which he said Russia used to transport weapons.

Zelenskyy said the Merkury, one of Russia’s newest warships, sank after Ukrainian forces launched seven naval drones on Sunday. A KA-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed in the attack, he said.

He confirmed that Ukraine’s forces also attacked the MV Angara, a cargo ship. Libya’s eastern health ministry said that all crew members had been rescued and were receiving treatment.

Authorities in eastern Libya said in a statement that the ship was docked in the port when the explosion occurred.

“The ship was en route back to Russia and its stop was for refuelling and resupply. It is suspected that the ship was attacked by drones”.

The United Nations has called for an independent investigation into Sunday’s drone attacks.

On Monday, the United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”.

“Libya cannot afford and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts,” UNSMIL wrote on X.

The eastern administration did not identify who was behind Sunday’s attack but said Libya was “not a party to the Russian-Ukrainian war”.

headline: Alcaraz storms past world number one Zverev to win maiden ATP Finals title
body:

The Spaniard, who returned at the US Open after a four-month break due to a wrist injury, saved three set points in the tiebreak before completing his 14th consecutive victory and ending the year with a ⁠third straight title, having also triumphed in Vienna and Paris.

The 23-year-old, who is the youngest man to have completed the career Grand Slam, secured the biggest tour title that had eluded him after finishing runner-up at the ATP Finals last year.

Since losing in the quarterfinals of the 2026 US Open, he has won four titles with a 22-1 record.

“For me, it’s been an amazing week,” ‌Alcaraz said. “I couldn’t have ended the week in a better way. I’m just really proud and really happy with everything I have done this week.

“I’ve been through really difficult moments within myself, with my team, and we went through everything playing great tennis. This trophy is something I have been chasing for a really long time.

“It means the world to me.”

For Zverev, the defeat brought an end to his most successful season, in which he won his first two Grand Slam titles and rose to the top of the world rankings.

Port Sudan, Sudan – In Sudan’s displacement camps, the stories of residents often follow similar paths, but each loss and hardship is a deeply personal experience.

Arafa Abdelaziz endured a dangerous 15-day journey from Omdurman to a displacement camp in Port Sudan in late 2023, after losing her husband and one of her two sons, who died early in the war.

Her husband died just days after fighting broke out between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in April 2023, leaving her to care for her remaining two children as their home city of Omdurman in Khartoum State came under bombardment.

Five months later, her eight-year-old son was killed by a stray bullet during clashes near Omdurman’s market.

“My son was playing outside the house with his friends when I suddenly heard a loud noise. When I went outside, I found that his head had been shattered by gunfire,” said the 33-year-old.

With the fighting between the SAF and RSF continuing in Omdurman, one of the centres of the power struggle between the two former allies at the start of the war, Arafa eventually decided to flee the city with her six-year-old son, who has a brain condition affecting his development.

She describes the journey to Port Sudan as a prolonged and horrifying ordeal. Near Jebel Aulia, south of Khartoum, RSF fighters intercepted the vehicle they were in and the passengers were robbed and assaulted.

“They asked every woman carrying a child how she wanted her son to be killed. I told them to kill me before they touched my son,” Arafa recalled.

When she confronted the fighters as they attempted to assault her child, one of them hit her with the butt of his rifle, leaving her unconscious for more than an hour.

“When I regained consciousness, I saw RSF fighters raping the young women who were travelling with us on the bus. Some were raped in front of their fathers. I felt it was the end,” she said.

In October 2026, UN Women reported that 12.7 million people, mostly women and girls, needed support for gender-based violence in Sudan – four times the pre-war figure.

The agency warned that sexual violence is being used as a weapon of war, with women and girls at risk while fleeing areas of fighting, in displacement camps and while searching for food, water and shelter.

Arafa said her greatest fear throughout the ordeal was for her younger son’s safety. When the fighters asked what valuables she had, she told them she owned nothing. They took two gold rings from her fingers and after severely beating her, let her continue her journey.

“I arrived in Port Sudan with nothing, having lost my husband. My son’s condition had worsened because of what we went through on the journey and because he could not receive his medication regularly,” she said.

It was Arafa’s first time in Port Sudan, so, having no family or friends there to support her, she headed to a school sheltering displaced families. She was later transferred to another displacement camp, where she now lives with her son. But reaching relative safety was not the end of her struggles. Her son’s condition fluctuates, and she remains worried about his health and future.

“Sometimes he imagines strange things because of his illness,” she said. “Yesterday, he told me he could see a lot of blood on the ground. It makes me think every day about his future with this condition.”

Arafa cannot afford his medication, so she has resorted to giving him medicine only when his condition deteriorates. She depends largely on aid distributed in the camp, as her needs and those of her son continue to grow.

“I’m afraid to leave him alone at home, out of my sight, in case he has a seizure or hurts himself,” she said.

The war in Sudan has killed as many as 150,000 people and forced millions from their homes, often to camps in impoverished neighbouring countries.

Income levels have dropped to 1992 levels and extreme poverty rates are worse than in the 1980s, according to the United Nations. Due to conscription, fatalities and emigration to other regions and countries for work, women have become the sole guardians in many displaced Sudanese households.

The UN’s 2025 Gender Snapshot found that 75 percent of female-headed households in Sudan were food insecure – three times the rate among male-headed households.

The Mashad Observatory has documented 72,202 cases of widowhood since the outbreak of war in Sudan in April 2023. That constitutes a complex humanitarian crisis which can lead to the collapse of household incomes, stability and protection systems. In the long term, it means transmitting deprivation, economic vulnerability and psychological trauma from one generation to the next.

These cumulative impacts can weaken social cohesion, exacerbate inequalities and undermine the capacity of local communities to recover from the consequences of war. This growing burden means fewer opportunities for women to work and increased dependence on humanitarian assistance, with long-term economic implications for Sudan, the group said.

“Their suffering is further compounded when women lose the primary source of household income or are forced to abandon their homes and communities without adequate financial resources or social support networks. Such circumstances may expose them to heightened risks of economic exploitation, gender-based violence, forced or early marriage involving their daughters and the interruption of their children’s education,” a spokesperson for the organisation told Al Jazeera.

“These pressures may also contribute to deteriorating mental health as a result of cumulative trauma, overwhelming responsibilities and the absence of appropriate psychosocial support services.”

With humanitarian agencies saying that Sudan’s 2026 response plan, which aims to reach 20.4 million people and requires $2.9bn, has received only 47% of the funding needed, there will be challenges in providing these families with the necessary support.

“Addressing this challenge therefore requires a transition from temporary emergency relief towards a comprehensive national strategy that places widows and female-headed households at the centre of Sudan’s recovery and reconstruction plans,” said the organisation.

“Such a strategy should include sustainable cash assistance, economic empowerment programmes, vocational training, access to decent employment, improved access to finance and productive enterprises, as well as guaranteed access to education, healthcare, legal protection and psychosocial support.”

Zahra Idris, 39, fled Khartoum with her husband and two children as shelling intensified, arriving in Port Sudan three years ago.

Her husband initially rented a house in the working-class neighbourhood of Al-Kasara. But when they could no longer afford the rent, the landlord evicted them. The family moved to a school shelter before being relocated to a displacement camp at the start of the school year.

Two months ago, Zahra’s husband died of heart disease, leaving her to care for their two children with little support beyond humanitarian assistance, which has become increasingly limited.

“Since my husband died, my fears have grown. I cannot go out to look for work until I complete the mourning period prescribed in Islam, which lasts four months and ten days,” she said.

Her 12-year-old son has an intellectual disability and requires regular medical care, something the family cannot afford given the rising cost of living.

“There is no one to help me. I just want my son’s condition to improve enough for him to attend a school for children with disabilities,” she said.

“Going from one organisation to another, looking for someone to cover my son’s medical treatment and education, cost me around 100,000 Sudanese pounds. That money could have covered our household needs for several days.”

headline: As Syria-EU talks progress, diplomats fear focus will be on repatriation
body:
Officials from Syria and the European Union are working on a deal to normalise relations after a 15-year suspension. But current and former European diplomats have told Al Jazeera they fear that growing right-wing sentiment in Europe could see efforts to repatriate Syrians and immigration being prioritised over other key issues, such as human rights.

Syrian and EU officials hope that a deal with the new government will lead to stronger trade and political relations, after a suspension following then-President Bashar al-Assad’s brutal crackdown on protesters in 2011.

With al-Assad’s regime overthrown and a government led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa seeking closer relations with Europe, there is an opportunity for diplomatic and trade relations to resume.

“The aim is to give Europe and Syria a framework for trade, political dialogue and closer cooperation as soon as possible,” Kaja Kallas, vice president of the European Commission, said in a statement on November 16. “Syria needs investment and a successful transition.”

Analysts and diplomats told Al Jazeera that Syria’s priority in the talks was the removal of lingering EU sanctions. Brussels is largely focused on the repatriation of Syrians, with more than a million fleeing to Europe during the Syrian war between 2011 and 2024. But they added that these issues must be managed carefully to avoid piling pressure on Syria as it continues to rebuild after the war and decades of dictatorship.

Officials from Syria and the European Union are working on a deal to normalise relations after a 15-year suspension. But current and former European diplomats have told Al Jazeera they fear that growing right-wing sentiment in Europe could see efforts to repatriate Syrians and immigration being prioritised over other key issues, such as human rights.

Syrian and EU officials hope that a deal with the new government will lead to stronger trade and political relations, after a suspension following then-President Bashar al-Assad’s brutal crackdown on protesters in 2011.

With al-Assad’s regime overthrown and a government led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa seeking closer relations with Europe, there is an opportunity for diplomatic and trade relations to resume.

“The aim is to give Europe and Syria a framework for trade, political dialogue and closer cooperation as soon as possible,” Kaja Kallas, vice president of the European Commission, said in a statement on November 16. “Syria needs investment and a successful transition.”

Analysts and diplomats told Al Jazeera that Syria’s priority in the talks was the removal of lingering EU sanctions. Brussels is largely focused on the repatriation of Syrians, with more than a million fleeing to Europe during the Syrian war between 2011 and 2024. But they added that these issues must be managed carefully to avoid piling pressure on Syria as it continues to rebuild after the war and decades of dictatorship.

“The migration issue is a big issue in Europe today,” Iyad Jaber, the Damascus-based head of Middle East at Timios & Co and former French diplomat of Syrian origin, told Al Jazeera. “Especially with right-wing and far-right wing [parties] taking more political space, it is moving political speech on migration.”

The first cooperation agreement between Europe and Syria was signed in 1978 by the EU’s predecessor, the European Economic Community (EEC), when Hafez al-Assad was Syria’s president. The agreement was focused on the economic and social development of Syria and a deepening of ties between the two parties.

In 2008, the EU-Syria Association Agreement was proposed but never signed by either side, largely due to concerns over the Assad government’s record on human rights. In 2011, when the government brutally repressed a popular uprising, the EU suspended ties with Syria.

During that time, the EU moved its diplomatic mission to Beirut and imposed sanctions on the Assad regime, freezing its assets and imposing travel bans on key officials.

Since the overthrow of the Assad regime, the EU has aimed to revive relations with the country. It lifted all economic sanctions on Syria last year, though some dual-use export controls and state institutions remain sanctioned.

In January, Brussels announced a two-year funding package of 620 million euros ($680m) for Syria and in May the EU held its first high-level political dialogue with Syria, which aimed to revive bilateral relations.

The EU’s diplomatic service prepared a discussion paper outlining the normalisation efforts. Al Jazeera reached out to the paper’s author, but she was unavailable for comment.

Kallas said diplomats are now working through technical and legal details to finalise the agreement, which would create frameworks for free trade, political dialogue and broader cooperation between Brussels and Damascus.

Many European nations have been exploring reopening embassies or missions in Syria, diplomats told Al Jazeera, while Syrian and EU officials continue talks on normalisation and sanctions removal.

Sally Shobat, Syria’s European Affairs Directorate at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, met Jonas Jonsson, head of the Middle East and North Africa Division at the European External Action Service, on Saturday, after earlier holding bilateral meetings with French, Cypriot and Belgian diplomatic officials.

Since the fall of the Assad government, Syria’s new government has worked to revive suspended relations and remove sanctions imposed on its predecessor. Many of the penalties have now been removed and relations with many countries, notably members of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and the United States, have also improved.

EU-Syrian relations may be moving in a positive direction, but experts said there are still many legal and technical obstacles to full normalisation.

“Every country has their own foreign policy,” Zakaria al-Shmaly, a nonresident fellow at TIMEP focusing on EU-Syria relations, told Al Jazeera.

Still, Syria has tried to prove its importance to Europe in security matters, particularly in the fight against ISIL (ISIS) and as an energy transit point following global disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

“Europe needs Syria as much as Syria needs Europe,” President al-Sharaa said in Nicosia in April, after an informal meeting between Syria and EU officials.

In April, al-Sharaa proposed the Four Seas and Nine Corridors Initiative, a proposed transatlantic framework connecting the Gulf, Caspian Sea, Mediterranean Sea and Black Sea via a Syria-Turkiye pipeline and transit corridor. The proposal bypasses the Strait of Hormuz for a land pipeline through Syria, following disruptions to shipping because of the US-Israel war on Iran, which began in February.

“Every power is using Syria to undermine Iran,” al-Shmaly said.

Another key point of discussion between the EU and Syria as normalisation talks continue will be trade. Experts said Brussels will likely try to open the Syrian market to EU products, which could benefit Syrian consumers by lowering costs on certain items. However, Syrian negotiators must also consider what kind of things Syrian companies can export to the EU.

“There are not a lot of Syrian exports,” Jaber told Al Jazeera. “They are mostly agricultural and some pharmaceutical, but there are not a lot of exports and this is what the Syrians need to be careful about; otherwise, they will open the market to a lot of European products while still facing barriers and tariffs on what they can export.”

Jaber said there is also room for EU-Syrian coordination on the issue of Assad regime assets, which could be worth tens of billions of dollars and “hidden in several parts of Europe”.

In the months following a change in government in Damascus, some European states paused asylum claims for Syrians, citing that the dangers from the war and former regime were over.

Migration and the presence of refugees have been a major political issue in Europe for over a decade, particularly as a number of countries experienced a growth in far-right parties or movements.

In her comments on November 16, Kallas addressed the future of human rights in Syria and decisions taken by the Assad regime. “Everybody said that we need to engage with Syria because if we don’t engage, then this vacuum will be filled by other players,” Kallas said. “We should have clear conditionality regarding human rights. We should have also the nonrecognition of occupied Ukrainian, Georgian territories that they have recognised under Assad’s regime.”

In recent years, al-Shmaly claimed that even governments on the political centre-ground had adopted increasingly extreme policies on immigration.

Current and former European diplomats told Al Jazeera they were concerned that Europe would overly focus on repatriation in any deal with Syria, leaving human rights and other important issues by the wayside.

“Structurally, we have a rising number of member states in the EU that are led by right-wing populists who see no interest in engaging in all of Syria’s complexity and challenges,” a former European diplomat, who requested to speak on background, told Al Jazeera.

“We tend to see Syria only through the very limited lens of migration and we also wrongly perceive Syrian refugees as a burden rather than an opportunity despite the fact that the overwhelming majority of Syrian refugees have very positively contributed to the European economy and culture.”

Since the fall of the Assad government, about one million Syrians have returned home, most from neighbouring countries such as Lebanon, Turkiye and Jordan. But experts said Europe must strike a delicate balance on migration due to the slow process of rebuilding the country after years of dictatorship and war.

“As the European Union deepens ties with Syria, returns cannot become the price of that relationship,” Tariq Azeez, the International Rescue Committee’s policy, advocacy and communications coordinator, told Al Jazeera.

“Our research shows the reality many Syrians are returning to: missing services, damaged housing and conditions worse than expected, and competition over scarce resources driving tension within communities. Accelerating returns, therefore, without investing in services for everyone, returnees and those who never left alike, risks fuelling exactly the instability Europe says it wants to prevent.”

Supporters of both countries, as well as neutral cricket fans, mingled in the stands while wearing their respective teams’ shirts, waving their own countries’ flags and chanting their players’ names.

The trend continued during India’s innings, which ended 48 runs short of the target, giving the Pakistanis a rare victory over their neighbours.

In the stands, though, the supporters were following a different script.

It took a few hours for the West End International Cricket Stadium to fill up – with Sunday being the first working day of the week in Qatar – but towards the second half of the match, the attendance came close to its 10,000-person capacity.

Supporters of both countries, as well as neutral cricket fans, mingled in the stands while wearing their respective teams’ shirts, waving their own countries’ flags and chanting their players’ names.

For many, such as Abrar Hussain and Mohammed Saeed Khan, there didn’t seem to be a need for segregation while watching a sport both nations follow with equal fervour.

“We have been friends for over six years,” Khan told Al Jazeera.

Wearing a replica blue shirt of the Indian team, Khan sat next to his Pakistani friend Hussain, dressed in Pakistan’s shirt.

“We share accommodation, meals and a love for the game that goes beyond any rivalry,” the man from India’s southern port metropolis of Mumbai explained.

Khan and Hussain, who are teammates in a weekend cricket league in Doha, expressed their disappointment at the “politicisation of the sport.”

“Politics should stay out of the game,” said Hussain, a native of Pakistan’s largest city, Karachi.

“The game of cricket is very close to our heart. We don’t want anything spoiling our game.”

Recent cricket encounters between the two nations – at all levels, from senior men’s teams to women’s sides, as well as age-group teams – have been heavily politicised following their intense four-day conflict last May.

Four months after both countries returned from the brink of all-out war, their cricket teams met in the Men’s Asia Cup 2025 and seemed to carry the bitterness of the conflict onto the field.

India’s players avoided shaking hands with Pakistanis, who made gestures linked to the cross-border aerial fight. The tournament ended with the victorious Indian team refusing to accept the trophy from the Pakistani head of the Asian Cricket Council.

The pattern has followed every India-Pakistan cricket encounter and even found its way into the Under-19 Asia Cup, where Indian players’ behaviour after sealing a win was heavily criticised.

Indian cricket fan Khan believes many players don’t want to partake in such aggression but are “forced into the act” at the behest of politicians and the younger generation is following suit.

“Cricket boards should take disciplinary action against [such] players and ensure that this behaviour is not passed on to the next generation.”

Khan’s teammate and good friend, Hussain, agreed.

“It is a worrying sign for the sport,” he said of the on-field antics.

“Politics has poisoned cricket and the fact that young cricketers show this behaviour is not good for the future of the game.”

The venue for the tournament in Qatar is in the heart of Asian Town, a Doha suburb inhabited by migrants from South Asia who work in the capital’s Industrial Area.

For several thousand workers, a tournament bringing their home nations to their neighbourhood is a welcome change from the everyday grind of their work lives.

To have these matches a short walk away from their accommodation is an added bonus.

However, the lure of an India-Pakistan cricket match brought fans from across the Gulf state.

Doha resident Avinash Daniel, originally from India’s capital New Delhi, brought along his young family and two friends after hearing about the fixture.

“It’s our first time watching an India-Pakistan match at a stadium and it’s been a great experience,” Daniel said.

Sweeping his gaze around the stand, he pointed out that a mix of Indian and Pakistani fans surrounded his group but they were happily mingling with each other.

“There are no different sides in the stands,” he said with a shrug. “No Indian stands, no Pakistani stands. We are all mixed. It’s a wonderful cultural experience.”

Daniel, a railway engineer, believed the politicisation of cricket only benefits politicians, not cricketers or fans, who only want to enjoy the sport that offers a brief respite to its billions of fans.

“At the end of this match, both Indians and Pakistanis will go out and eat the same mandi – a traditional Arab rice and meat dish – probably cooked and served by Indians and Pakistanis.”

full:
Hailed as ‘a rare moment of justice’, judges’ decision sets out a roadmap for assessing the question of intent

The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states.

In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent.

The lengthy judgment will have been read particularly carefully by Israel, the only other country currently before the ICJ accused of genocide.

It is also relevant to Germany, which has been brought before the court by Nicaragua on the accusation it has facilitated and failed to prevent genocide in Gaza.

“I think it’s a judgment that brings the genocide convention alive,” said Philippe Sands, a leading human rights lawyer who was part of the Gambian legal team. “It gives the convention practical, real meaning. And if the alternative view had been taken, the convention would essentially become a dead letter.”

Amnesty International’s secretary general, Agnès Callamard, called the ruling “a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families”. But it was also an assertion of humanitarian law in an increasingly lawless world.

“This is a good day for international law. We needed it,” said Dr Iva Vukušić, an assistant professor in international History at Utrecht University and a war crimes expert. “It is really important, clarifying a lot of law, and that’s going to be very helpful going forward.”

There will be a spillover from this ruling to its sister tribunal in The Hague, the international criminal court (ICC), providing a benchmark for when genocide charges could be made against individual perpetrators.

The Trump administration, instinctively hostile to international legal institutions, is also watching critically. The US ambassador to the UN told the ICJ before this judgment not to “lower the legal threshold for proving genocide” lest it be “weaponised” against US and allied soldiers.

The court did not directly lower the standard for demonstrating genocide, and the Gambia – which brought the case to The Hague – did not ask it to.

The judges kept the existing benchmark for judging genocide intent as the “only reasonable inference” of Myanmar’s actions and referred extensively to prior case law. But it went a long way towards clarifying how that standard should be applied in assessing atrocity crimes committed by states.

Before this case, only Serbia had faced the charge of genocide at the ICJ, in cases brought by Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the Bosnian ruling in 2007, Belgrade was found to have failed to prevent the 1995 genocide in Srebrenica, but in both cases it was cleared of committing the genocide directly.

The new ICJ judgment finds the Myanmar military directly responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, a Muslim minority targeted in a ferocious counterinsurgency campaign that reached its peak in 2017.

In assessing the Myanmar campaign, the ICJ looked not just at the death toll of about 10,000 in assessing the scale of the atrocities, but at the total Rohingya population targeted in northern Rakhine state, 815,000 people. Significantly, it cast its net wider than just the death toll, considering mental damage done to the survivors, particularly victims of sexual violence, and the impact on reproduction in the Rohingya community.

Most importantly, the ICJ judgment provided a guide to interpreting the standard set by Serbian cases, in which a finding of genocide could be made only if there were not other plausible motives for mass killing.

In this judgment, the court ruled that Myanmar could have had other motives, such as the desire to displace or punish the Rohingya population, but that those motives could exist alongside genocidal intent. The judges said genocidal intent was the “only reasonable inference” from the “totality” of evidence.

In justifying that conclusion the judges pointed to several factors that international law experts say are relevant to the Gaza case, which is now hearing written pleadings and is expected to take at least another three years.

The common factors include the targeting of children, which the court described as striking at the “foundation” of the Rohingya as a group – the ICJ said up to 2,109 Rohingya children under the age of five had been killed, while more than 5,000 Palestinian children under five years old have been killed in the Gaza war.

Another incriminating factor cited by the court was the “bulldozing and large-scale terrain clearance” after the destruction of villages, followed by “rapid construction” including security installations, which has been the hallmark of Israeli army occupation of over 60% of the Gaza Strip.

“It’s full of messages for Israel,” said William Schabas, an international law professor and expert on genocide at Middlesex University. “There are obvious differences, of course, the evidence will be different, but if you exchanged the word Myanmar with Israel, you wouldn’t have to change much in the judgment.”

The fact that there were six dissenting voices on the bench suggested that substantial parts of the majority’s reasoning were not beyond dispute, and lawyers involved in the case cautioned that it did not necessarily mean that the same bench would find Israel guilty of genocide in Gaza. But the same lawyers added that the opposite was almost certainly true. If this case had failed, the case brought by South Africa against Israel would have been all but over.

headline: Up to 1.1m people eligible to join class action against Jetstar over alleged failure to refund Covid flights
body:
Jetstar accused of issuing customers credits instead of cash refunds for flights cancelled between 2020 and late 2022

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

More than 1 million Jetstar customers could be eligible to join a class action alleging the airline failed to refund them for flights it cancelled during the pandemic, the firm leading the lawsuit has said.

The federal court on Monday confirmed it had ordered notices be sent to customers informing them of their eligibility to participate in, or opt out of, the lawsuit, with a potential trial set for March 2027.

Echo Law, the firm leading the class action, said it wanted to alert the public to the notices – which were due to be distributed by 4 December – to ensure they understood it was not a scam. About 1.1 million people will receive them.

The class action alleges Jetstar issued customers flight credits instead of the cash refunds they were entitled to for flights cancelled between 2020 and late 2022, after cancelling thousands of scheduled domestic and international flights.

Echo Law ran a separate class action against Qantas over its handling of Covid-19 travel credits, which the airline in March agreed to settle for $105m with no admission of liability.

In its case against Jetstar, the firm alleges the airline breached its legal obligations to customers by failing to provide refunds for cancelled flights, instead offering customers credit vouchers.

after newsletter promotion

“During the Covid-19 pandemic, Jetstar took a range of steps to respond to rapidly changing travel restrictions, while continuing to support customers affected by disruptions,” a spokesperson for the airline said.

“We provided customers with a range of options during this period depending on the circumstances, including travel credits, fee-free flight changes and refunds.”

They said the Jetstar Covid-19 vouchers remained valid as the airline had removed the expiry date in 2023.

However, Andrew Paull, a partner at Echo Law, alleged Jetstar’s policy of “pushing” customers to accept vouchers was designed to preserve the airline’s cash position.

“It held onto ordinary Australian’s [sic] money and expected customers to just be happy with credits, or in some cases nothing, when we allege they were entitled to cash refunds,” he alleged.

Paull alleged many customers had ended up paying Jetstar more than their original booking to use their credits on new fares, as they were led to believe they had little choice but to do so in order to avoid losing the value of their flights.

The firm’s lawsuit against Jetstar is scheduled for mediation in December and is expected to go to trial if the parties fail to reach an agreement.

Echo Law said the litigation funder Court House Capital was backing its class action against Jetstar.

Court House Capital’s chief investment officer, Heather Collins, accused Jetstar of seeking to “delay resolution while continuing to hold onto money that belongs to Australian families”.

headline: Netanyahu rival condemns ‘Jewish terrorism’ after settler attacks on Palestinian villages
body:
Dozens of militant Israeli settlers raided communities on Saturday night, setting fire to vehicles and several homes

Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank have caused a political row in Israel, drawing condemnation from Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader, who described them as “Jewish terrorism”.

Dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday, setting fire to about a dozen vehicles and several homes and scrawling racist graffiti. At least four communities were attacked. Israeli police said they had launched an investigation with forensic teams.

Photographs from Kafr Malik, near Ramallah, showed one slogan written in Hebrew that read: “This is the first revenge.” Several vehicles and homes had been set alight in the village.

Images from nearby Deir al-Sudan showed vehicles on fire. Palestinian reports said an agricultural building had been set ablaze in Deir Ballut and cars torched in Deir Abu Mashal.

An ⁠inconclusive election last month stripped Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, of his majority. Eisenkot has been asked to form a government, though his prospects seem little better.

“Last night’s arson attacks in Judea and Samaria were acts of Jewish terrorism, in every sense of the term,” Eisenkot said, using the biblical name for the West Bank. “Extremist groups that set fire to vehicles and homes are undermining regional stability, putting lives at risk and doing grave damage to Israel’s national security and foreign relations.”

In an unprecedented rebuke on Sunday, several other members of the Israeli parliament criticised Netanyahu over escalating violence by militant settlers against Palestinians.

Yair Lapid, the leader of Yesh Atid, held Netanyahu’s government responsible for encouraging the attacks. “Jewish terrorism is the product of criminal negligence by the Israeli government,” he said on X, adding that ministers were deliberately encouraging the militant settlers’ violence “through their silence”.

Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats party, warned of the possibility of a third intifada and described the West Bank as “on the brink of an explosion”.

“Anyone who wants to prevent a third intifada must replace the current government, which provides cover and support for Jewish terrorism and abandons security,” Golan said on X. “Jewish terrorism harms innocent Palestinians and Israeli army soldiers, and pushes Israel toward unprecedented international isolation.”

Noam Tibon, a retired army major general and Knesset member, gave a similar warning. “If Israel does not eliminate Jewish terrorism in the West Bank, it will destroy Israel,” he wrote.

Netanyahu has not yet responded to the accusations.

Australia announced sanctions on Wednesday against three people and four Israeli entities, including a construction company, over their role in the expansion of illegal settlements and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

A day earlier the UK imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building illegal settlements in the West Bank, which the UN regards as Palestinian territory under Israeli occupation since 1967.

Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.

On Tuesday, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman was shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli militant settlers in a village near Jericho, where the group has recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.

headline: Abdul El-Sayed doubles down on ‘TrumpCare’ health plan, urging president to ‘get it done’
body:
Democratic senator-elect reiterates suggestion to rename Medicare for All after Trump if president allows bill to pass

Michigan US senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday doubled down on naming healthcare reform legislation after Donald Trump as long as it meant the president would not impede its passage.

“If he’s open to the conversation, I am open to it, too,” El-Sayed said of Trump on Sunday. “If the president is opening to signing that bill, let’s get it done.”

El-Sayed made those remarks on Sunday on NBC’s Meet the Press, where he reiterated his pledge to pursue a single-payer, national healthcare program after the Democrat became the first Muslim person elected to the US Senate during the midterms earlier in November.

Trump’s Republican party is going to lose control of Congress for the second half of his second presidency. But the president has made clear his intention to wield his legislative veto powers whenever he sees fit.

Appearing on Sunday’s Meet the Press, El-Sayed said he would not mind Medicare for All – a big part of his campaign platform – being named “TrumpCare” as long as such a program came into existence.
