Trump’s Republican party is going to lose control of Congress for the second half of his second presidency. But the president has made clear his intention to wield his legislative veto powers whenever he sees fit.

Appearing on Sunday’s Meet the Press, El-Sayed said he would not mind Medicare for All – a big part of his campaign platform – being named “TrumpCare” as long as such a program came into existence.

“I care that the people of this country finally have the unmet promise of guaranteed healthcare in this country. And if the president is serious about leaving a lasting legacy, there is nothing better than the ultimate Trump card,” El-Sayed said to Meet the Press host Kristen Welker, making a double entendre for a term that – when the T is lowercase – also refers to a card that beats out others in card games.

El-Sayed told Welker that such a Trump card would be in effect “from the moment [people] are born to the moment that they pass away – that guarantees them the healthcare that has been so elusive in this country without premiums, co-pays and deductibles”.

The senator-elect’s comments come after he previously suggested to CNN that he is not above stroking Trump’s prodigious ego to get legislation passed – including by naming Medicare for All “TrumpCare”.

He also previously wrote on social media, alongside images of a gold health insurance card with “TrumpCare” inscribed on it: “Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”

Trump seemingly responded to El-Sayed’s post by reposting a screenshot of the senator-elect’s tweet. Trump has not formally responded to the push to create universal healthcare.

Trump has spent much of his second presidency trying to get as much as possible named after him – from institutions, physical buildings and currency.

El-Sayed also said that he supports healthcare reform proposed by Bernie Sanders, the progressive US senator.

Sanders’ proposal would create a single-payer system in which the federal government insures everybody, financed by an increase in taxes, while eliminating private insurance.

But El-Sayed said he is not focused on eliminating private insurance as an option, which Sanders aims to eliminate by having everything primary and preventive services to hospital stays covered under his proposed plan. Out-of-pocket costs on deductibles and co-pays – staples of the rapacious private insurance industry to which most Americans must resort – would also be eliminated under Sanders’ plan.

El-Sayed said he wants to “provide you basic public health insurance no matter who you are in this country” while being open to the idea of not taking alternative options away.

The senator-elect said he has a meeting on the books with JD Vance. El-Sayed would not share the agenda of the meeting, but he confirmed that the vice-president’s chief of staff contacted him after his election victory.

“There’s no doubt the accused, Beau Lamarre-Condon, did plenty of foolish things and you might think the level of them was unusual, that he was a poorly behaved boyfriend.

“There’s a long distance between his admitting that sort of behaviour, and you finding him guilty of murder.”

But crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC urged the jury to reject Lamarre-Condon’s account and convict him on all three counts, as he finished his closing statement on Monday.

“The case is that the accused, driven by this jealous obsession, drove to Paddington in a hire car, scoped the house and waited for his opportunity,” he told the court.

Lamarre-Condon entered the house with a gun loaded with stolen bullets, and shot Baird in the back and temple, Hatfield alleged.

“It was not self-defence or an accident,” he said. “The evidence speaks only to an execution.”

Lamarre-Condon had testified he shot Baird after he lunged at him with a knife.

During this struggle, his gun was then flung across the room and picked up by Davies before the officer grabbed his arm and pushed the gun towards Davies.

Davies then pulled the trigger and shot himself, Lamarre-Condon told the court.

after newsletter promotion

But this defence rests entirely on his own account and even if Baird had picked up a knife, it would not have assisted him against a Glock pistol, Hatfield said.

“You might think he is a proven and persistent liar and such a scenario is completely contrary to the weight of the evidence,” he told the court.

“The accused’s account is not the truth. It is a story made up after the fact in an attempt to meet the evidence.”

The prosecution also failed to locate the bullet or any bullet fragments of the shot that struck Davies, and this is enough to leave jurors with reasonable doubt about the crown case, the barrister said.

headline: ‘Everyone struggled for this justice’: tears in court as Rohingya vindicated in Myanmar genocide ruling
body:
Relief in the immediate aftermath of a landmark ruling, but what happens next is in the hands of governments around the world

There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them.

For almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape. More than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.

By the time they spilled into the court’s halls, the relief was evident. A Rohingya community leader threw a big thumbs up as he left the courtroom and others immediately took out their phones to call family in the refugee camps.

Salma, 30, a Rohingya survivor who lost family members in the 2017 genocide, said: “Everyone worked hard and struggled for this justice, for this cause. When they hear it today, everyone will be happy, thank God. I don’t know how to express it or even what to do with myself.”

Another Rohingya present, who cannot be named because of safety concerns, said they cried as the judge went through each of the rulings.

Another Rohingya present, who cannot be named because of safety concerns, said they cried as the judge went through each of the rulings.

“During the last few minutes I couldn’t even sit down any more, I had to move to the back because I didn’t know how I’d react,” they said. “I saw some of the other Rohingya around me crying. They were so emotional.

“Now the responsibility is with the international governments. It has been declared genocide now and they have to act.”

In Bangladesh, where most of the Rohingya population have lived – in the world’s largest refugee camp – since being forced to flee in 2017, the verdict was translated into the Rohingya language for the crowds who had gathered to watch on screens specially set up for the purpose.

They immediately leapt up, cheering, applauding and shouting gratitude for the Gambia – the faraway African nation that brought the case to the ICJ on behalf of the stateless minority. Many held posters that read “Thank You Gambia” and “Justice = Safe Return”.

“Since we arrived here, we have been waiting and looking forward to this justice,” said Farida Khatun, 50, who has been a refugee in Bangladesh since 2017, when her village, Tula Toli, was targeted by soldiers. The village in north-western Myanmar, near the Bangladesh border, was the scene of a massacre in August of that year, with reports of mass killings and gang rapes.

She said, however, that she does not expect to be able to return home. Tula Toli was completely destroyed by Myanmar’s forces and no longer exists. “Even though today’s verdict makes us happy, my heart still cannot believe that they will take us back in true peace.”

The case has taken seven years to reach this point, with Rohingya researchers working to collect testimony from survivors. The initial hope for justice had faded during the long wait for a ruling. Many were also left deflated during early hearings when the one-time pro-democracy hero Aung San Suu Kyi defended the Myanmar military at The Hague.

Before today’s ruling, some were optimistic, others were prepared to be disappointed, but all said they knew themselves that they were victims of genocide.

The tension was finally released when the court declared Myanmar was responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, highlighting the use of sexual violence and attacks on children alongside the killing of Rohingya who tried to flee violence, which it said meant the violence amounted to more than ethnic cleansing.

The court ordered Myanmar to provide reparations for the Rohingya and end continuing breaches of the genocide convention.

There is now also an international criminal court investigation into the violence of 2017, looking specifically at the crime of mass deportation, and for which prosecutors in 2024 sought an arrest warrant for Myanmar’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing.

With continuing violence against the Rohingya, the possibility of a return to Myanmar, as happened after previous exoduses to Bangladesh in 1978 and the early 1990s, remains unlikely.

But many hope the ICJ ruling will be the start of a process of ensuring justice and lead to real international pressure to ensure their safety in Myanmar.

“We will be able to return to our homeland – with our rights, with our citizenship, and having received our full security. We will be able to return,” says Salma.

headline: Indian opposition party’s youth wing warns of more Meta protests after police clashes
body:
Members of Congress party clashed with police outside tech company’s offices on Friday

The youth wing of India’s main opposition Congress party warned of more protests against Meta’s removal of some of its members’ ⁠accounts, ⁠a day after clashing with ​police outside the tech firm’s locals offices.

In Hyderabad on Friday, protesters ‌carrying placards and chanted slogans as they stormed into ‌the building that houses Meta’s offices, smashing plants to the ground and clashing with police, according to footage released by the Indian Youth Congress’s X account.

The Indian Youth Congress on Saturday posted warnings on X that it would “storm your offices across the country and stage protests” unless the Instagram accounts of its leaders were restored.

Two such accounts were restored after Friday’s protests, but thousands of accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government remain restricted, Manu Jain, who is in charge of social media for ⁠the youth group, told Reuters on Saturday. Meta must explain how its algorithms restrict posts and must restore accounts taken down ​on government orders, he added.

India is Meta’s biggest market by users and the company declined to comment on Friday’s demonstrations.

Debate is growing in India about potential ⁠risks to free speech from the increasingly strict efforts of Narendra Modi’s government to remove social media content it objects to. India’s IT ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Meta has said it restricts ​content in India to comply with local laws.

headline: Gas prices in Europe surge as forecast cold snap feeds supply shortage fears
body:

European gas prices surged on Monday as a forecast cold snap in the coming weeks fed fears across the continent’s over depleted supply this winter and costly household bills.

The Dutch month-ahead contract – the European benchmark for gas prices over the next four weeks– rose by as much as 8.6% to €96.08, before settling up 4% at €92.50.

The jump in gas prices comes as much of north-west Europe braces for a tough winter, when energy demand is at its highest.

Europe’s gas supplies have been hit by a slowdown in exports from Qatar due to the war in the Middle East, as well as an increase in consumption during the summer to power refrigeration and cooling during the prolonged heatwave.

Storage levels on the continent are now well below the seasonal average, at about 69% full against a typical level of 80%.

In the UK, energy system operators have said the country will have enough gas and electricity to meet demand during the coldest months, partly because of paying higher market prices than neighbours to secure imports.

However, it means British households will probably pay some of the highest energy bills in Europe this winter.

headline: Constitutional law expert brands defence bill allowing secret security rules ‘lazy and irresponsible’
body:

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

Labor’s new defence bill is “lazy and irresponsible” lawmaking, one of Australia’s leading constitutional scholars has warned, claiming provisions for the government to secretly class any facility as a special security zone could raise serious legal issues.

In a video on her YouTube channel, Twomey – professor emerita at the University of Sydney – claimed it was “flabbergasting that it was not the subject of proper debate or scrutiny before this law was enacted”.

“This notion of permitting secret alterations to commonwealth, state and territory laws is a really serious development.”

Anne Twomey says lack of proper debate around bill is ‘flabbergasting’ amid concerns over extension of ministerial powers

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

Labor’s new defence bill is “lazy and irresponsible” lawmaking, one of Australia’s leading constitutional scholars has warned, claiming provisions for the government to secretly class any facility as a special security zone could raise serious legal issues.

But parliamentary crossbenchers opposed to the bill, which was rushed through parliament with little public scrutiny, were joined on Monday by Prof Anne Twomey, who expressed alarm about what she called an increasing trend of ministers exercising discretionary powers without parliamentary oversight.

“Yes, it’s important we have defence legislation that’s flexible to deal with uncertain times, but let’s remember we’re trying to defend our democratic system of government, and we don’t want to throw it out at the same time,” Twomey told Guardian Australia.

In a video on her YouTube channel, Twomey – professor emerita at the University of Sydney – claimed it was “flabbergasting that it was not the subject of proper debate or scrutiny before this law was enacted”.

“This notion of permitting secret alterations to commonwealth, state and territory laws is a really serious development.”

The wide-ranging bill criminalises entering or photographing a defence security zone or a person or thing within, entering or leaving it, with a maximum penalty of up to seven years’ jail time, a $152,880 fine, or both. Security zones can include regular defence bases but can also extend to emergency, temporary or mobile sites as decided by a minister, with wide-ranging powers to “effectively do anything”.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

The minister can make a “capability declaration”, which allows for certain activity to be carried out “without contravening certain other laws, or changes the way that other laws apply” – including state and territory laws. Such a declaration can also be held back from being declared as a legislative instrument.

After passing the Senate last week, the final bill passed the lower house on Monday evening. Labor and the Coalition supported the bill, with only a handful of crossbenchers – including Kate Chaney, Monique Ryan and Andrew Wilkie – resisting.

The Greens, David Pocock, Digital Rights Watch and other civil society groups also strongly opposed the bill. But Albanese, in his first public comments on the legislation, said “people shouldn’t jump at shadows”, claiming the powers were necessary and “just practical”.

“It will be accountable obviously for things that are designated, but we live in unsafe times,” he said on Monday.

“I find it remarkable in 2026, there’s a question over whether we need to designate areas as being protected. And we live in times where we know there are more conflicts in the world today than at any time since world war two.”

The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, called the changes “extreme wartime powers” and “an assault on civil liberties”, claiming people may be charged for breaking laws they were not even aware of.

after newsletter promotion

Pocock said Albanese’s response was “disingenuous”.

“We need to protect sensitive defence facilities from threats posed by drones and other technologies. But that doesn’t mean handing the defence minister extraordinary powers without proper safeguards,” he told Guardian Australia.

“At a bare minimum, far stronger safeguards are needed around the use of ministerial powers, the need to protect civil liberties and greater transparency.”

Twomey, in her video, branded the legislation “quite disturbing”, noting declarations could be made secretly – which she said raised “serious rule of law issues” – and called out what she said was a concerning movement of giving ministers more discretionary power.

“Instead of working out what laws need to change to accommodate defence needs and then balancing them against the needs and rights of the community, the parliament has effectively just given up and instead given the power to the minister or indeed senior public servants or defence officers to make decisions that exclude the application of existing laws to defence activities.

“This is a lazy and irresponsible abandonment by parliament of both its scrutiny and its lawmaking roles, raising the risk that these powers will be misused in the future.”

headline: Trump threatens ‘tremendous penalties’ for US tech firms that build datacenters abroad
body:
President gives wide-ranging White House press conference and says he has ‘fantastic relationships’ with Putin and Xi

Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.

In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.

Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.

At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.

“We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said.

He said Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.

“You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he said.

Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.

In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.

Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.

At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.

“We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said.

He said Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.

“You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he said.

“We want them to build it here.”

With many Americans turning against the datacenters being built near their homes, the US tech industry is making a show of conciliation by promising to take fewer government handouts, to be more transparent, and to give more money to towns and cities willing to allow server warehouses to be built.

The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced US computing chips and servers, in a move it said was designed to limit China’s ability to use US chips to train its artificial intelligence models – though a House committee said on Wednesday the US had signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months.

China’s ability to obtain advanced AI chips made by the US firm Nvidia, in which Trump is an investor, has been spotlighted in recent weeks after its CEO, Jensen Huang, was fired over his affair with a woman alleged to be spying for China.

In the same press conference, Trump was asked about reports Iran was planning to potentially detonate an explosive laced with nuclear material – a so-called “dirty bomb” – in Washington DC. The president called it a “rumour” and said: “If they do, we’re going to fight.”

He added: “We know a lot about what’s happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We’ll find out about it.”

Responding to a question about reports of a rift with Vance, Trump said the vice-president’s remark blaming the Republican collapse on the Iran war was “a very accurate statement”.

“I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” the president said. “I would have added one other thing if it were asked … would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”

Trump was asked whether Vladimir Putin could really be considered a friend to America since Russia is a close ally of Iran.

“I can’t speak to America,” he said, adding: “I consider [that] I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that.”

He praised Putin as he repeated his grievances over the Department of Justice’s investigation into the Russian attempts to influence US voters ahead of the 2016 presidential election.

“I’ve been dealing with Putin … [since] the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax,” he said.

Trump also spoke about two prominent Democrats. He said Gina Hinojosa, who won the race for Texas governor over Trump’s Republican ally Greg Abbott, called him. “She was really nice,” Trump said. “It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border, and I think we’ll be able to work something out.”

And he said Hakeem Jeffries – who Trump previously called a “thug” but is now in line to be the next speaker of the House, and the first Black speaker – is “a smart guy. He’s a streetwise guy.”

headline: Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling
body:
A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza

Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.

It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.

The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.

A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza

Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.

It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.

The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.

The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.

Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.

The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.

The US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also announced sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.

The Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize. She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.

Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.

Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians.”

In remarks addressed to Pillay, he said: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”

In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”

after newsletter promotion

He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.

Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.

In the Myanmar case, a 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states, argued that the ICJ, in judging intent to commit genocide, should examine a range of “facts and circumstances” assessed “comprehensively and holistically”.

It also stressed that genocide was not solely defined by killings, and that the treatment of children, gender-based violence and forced displacement were also relevant.

The US until recently had taken a relatively more benign view of The Hague-based ICJ, and under Antony Blinken as US secretary of state determined that Myanmar had committed genocide.

The 15 ICJ judges are elected for nine-year terms by the UN security council and the UN general assembly.

Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before he imposes sanctions.

On Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan. The shelving of the near-dormant inquiry came after it was agreed evidence would be hard to obtain, but one side-effect may be a greater willingness on the part of the US to abandon its plan to impose sanctions on the ICC.

Trade minister hopes EU trade deal will pass parliament early next year

The trade minister, Don Farrell, says he hopes Australia’s free trade deal with the European Union will pass parliament early in 2027.

Farrell was interviewed on the ABC’s Afternoon Briefing program a short time ago, where he was asked about the deal.

After almost a decade of negotiations, Labor hammered out a deal with the EU in March, expected to mean 98% of Australia’s goods exported to the EU will enter duty-free and be worth an initial $10bn a year.

The deal contains a commitment to respect the Paris climate agreement, which Australia is already a signatory to.

Despite Farrell previously having warned there is no room to renegotiate the agreement, the Coalition has said it will not support the legislation required to enact the deal.

Today, Farrell said he had “not given up on anyone” supporting the legislation’s passage through parliament, which he hoped would occur “early in the new year”.

We’re just waiting for the final documentation to come to us from the Europeans.

I’m increasingly confident that the majority of senators will support this agreement.

I’m discussing with everybody, every senator in the parliament … my door is open to all the senators who have questions

You can read more about the deal, and the Coalition’s fight over it, here:

Alastair Campbell, former Blair spin doctor, challenges Australian media to be braver

Australians shouldn’t sit easy with Pauline Hanson receiving millions in donations, a sweetheart real-estate deal and a private jet from the country’s richest person, according to one of the world’s most popular political pundits, AAP reports.

Alastair Campbell, the arch spin doctor for former UK Labour prime minister Tony Blair turned co-host of the Rest is Politics podcast, has challenged the Australian media to be braver and improve their offering for young people.

Speaking to an audience of reporters at Canberra’s National Press Club earlier today, Campbell said:

I’m overwhelmingly critical of the media and what it’s become over my lifetime but ... my criticism comes from a place of love.

Campbell criticised what he said was journalists’ failure to properly scrutinise populists, and convince younger generations there was anything to gain from political involvement.

When the politicians are driven by the populism of my definition – politics as problem exploitation, not problem solving – then the media should expose and challenge the populists, not ventriloquise.

Is it too much to expect journalists to stand up for each other once in a while in defence of the legitimate role they play?

NSW Greens ask candidates not to interrupt opponents’ press conferences

The NSW Greens have issued a statement reminding their candidates not to interrupt their political opponents’ press conferences after heckling by upper house candidate Shane Bazzi led to the premier, Chris Minns, cancelling an event this morning.

Bazzi, who is fourth placed on the Greens ticket in the March ballot, crashed a media appearance in the marginal electorate of East Hills, shouting at Minns about making “captain’s calls” on Labor preselections, the war in Gaza and the government’s treatment of protesters.

In a statement, a spokesperson for the NSW Greens said:

As we enter the election period we will remind candidates that while we may sometimes strongly disagree with the views of our political opponents, we generally don’t interrupt their press conferences.

At a reconvened press conference this morning, Minns said there was a difference between “a candidate and a regular punter, a member of the public”, saying:

When you’re an MP and someone comes along in a media conference or on a street walk and has their say, you’ve got to take your hits, and that is part of the political process ... I just think there’s a distinction [with] political candidates getting their two cents in.

A gay New South Wales MP has backtracked on his request for the deeply conservative politician, the Rev Fred Nile, to be honoured with a state funeral, after blowback from the LGBTQ+ community, AAP reports.

Nile, an ordained Christian minister who was a member of NSW parliament for more than 40 years, died aged 92 on Saturday.

He was known for his staunch opposition to drug use, gay marriage and abortion.

Alex Greenwich, the member for Sydney, had praised the controversial politician on Sunday and suggested a state funeral.

But Greenwich, whose electorate takes in Australia’s gay heartland of Sydney’s Oxford St, backpedalled on Monday, saying that:

I’m sorry. I’ve listened, read your comments and emails, and recognise that my requests for a state service for Rev Fred Nile caused hurt and distress, particularly within the LGBTQ community.

While we worked constructively together towards the end of his life, and he apologised for past harm and supported LGBTQ reforms, this does not erase the pain and discrimination caused by his earlier campaigns.

I’ll hand you over to the brilliant Catie McLeod and see you back here bright and early tomorrow.

Angus Taylor was out for scalps today, calling for the resignation of Chris Bowen over his “Cop flop” and of treasurer Jim Chalmers.

Anthony Albanese and Chalmers retaliated, defending their budget and economic position, while acknowledging that times were tough.

Dan Tehan was the first and only MP to get kicked out of the chamber, after he tried to use a Molly Meldrum catchphrase against the government.

The $6m golf club grant in Albanese’s electorate was back in the spotlight – he wouldn’t answer a question about whether he misled over his claims his membership was only worth $5 and that the grant was for sewage works – both which were disputed by the club.

Independent Andrew Wilkie called for more action to clear people needing an aged care bed or NDIS support from hospitals.

And while Helen Haines wasn’t in parliament (and is not expected back until next year), the crossbench placed an orange cockatoo on her seat in her honour.

Jim Chalmers has warned Australians that “things will get a bit harder before they get easier”, revealing next month’s budget update will show unemployment climbing above 5% alongside slower economic growth for the next two years.

The treasurer is making a ministerial address to the House now.

My colleague, Patrick Commins, has it covered here:

‘It takes two to tango’: Coalition won’t rush gas reservation scheme negotiations

As deliberations between Labor and the Coalition continue on a gas reservation policy, Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, says the opposition won’t be pressured by “some artificial timeline”.

It takes two to tango. Here we’ve been very constructive.

We put specific amendments to the government. We’ve written and drafted those. If the government doesn’t support them, we’ll move those and have the debate in the chamber.

The two major parties remain locked in talks over a proposal to set up a federal scheme that would require Australia’s largest gas exporters to set aside up to 20% of their product for domestic use.

With only three parliamentary sitting days left, time is running out to pass legislation this year.

The opposition remains the party of choice for Labor to negotiate a deal with, as the Greens demand a 25% tax on gas exports in return for their support.

Question time ends early after fiery dixer

Well, that ended quickly.

The PM just called time on QT after a particularly heated dixer to Tanya Plibersek.

She was asked how the digital duty of care bill will “help tackle family, domestic and sexual violence”.

She took the opportunity to accuse the Coalition of allowing online violence to continue because they won’t support the digital reforms.

It had the Coalition in an absolute uproar.

While we know that rates of sexual violence are exploding, we’ve got the Liberals, the Nationals and One Nation not prepared to vote to support a digital duty of care – particularly for our children. They’re continuing to say that young Australians should be exposed to things like violent pornography, including depictions of incest and strangulation, or content on how to get away with grooming.

She’s told to “reflect on her language” by the speaker, but ends saying, “members opposite should be ashamed” for not supporting the bill.

Just three to go.

Independent Helen Haines, who lost both her legs and is in rehabilitation after she was allegedly struck by a vehicle, isn’t in parliament today.

But her presence is still felt.

The crossbench have put an orange cockatoo on her seat to honour her.

Wilkie calls for action to clear patients from hospital beds waiting for aged care and NDIS

Back to the crossbench, independent Andrew Wilkie asks the health, NDIS and aged care minister, Mark Butler, about the number of people in hospital beds who are waiting for an aged care or NDIS place.

He says in his state of Tasmania, nearly 10% of public hospital beds are occupied by people awaiting residential aged care placements or appropriate NDIS supports, and asks what the government will do to fix this.

Butler starts by outlining the scope of the problem:

15 years ago, about 15,000 Australians turned 80 every year. Next year, it will be 90,000 – an increase of 500%.

Butler lists the $25bn of funding the federal government has provided the states to beef up the primary care system, as well as increased funding for aged care support at home places. He says that’s helping the situation but it’s still not ideal.

I think even the minister in Tasmania would accept that the work we’ve done – which started under Minister [Bill] Shorten – to put in place NDIS planners in hospitals have dramatically reduced the wait time for people ready for discharge into an NDIS place.

I accept the challenge really is in aged care. The numbers are increasing dramatically. Our ability to build aged care facilities not improving as quickly as I would like. I want to continue working with state governments, including Tasmania’s, to improve that.

Albanese on the back foot on golf club grant

We’re back to the Marrickville golf club grant, folks.

The plot thickened recently after it was revealed by the general manager of the club that the prime minister’s honorary membership was not worth $5 as Anthony Albanese claimed, but $1,100, and that the $6m grant was not for sewerage works.

Deputy Nationals leader, Darren Chester asks: “Isn’t this just another reason why Australians don’t trust this prime minister? I give the call to the prime minister.”

Albanese doesn’t answer the question, but instead defends his other prior claim that he had no idea about the honorary membership.

He quotes general manager Mathew Ward:

He said this: ‘I went through it extensively. It wasn’t the practice at the time, and in the board minutes, to name the new members. There’s no mention of it in the board minutes. There was a club newsletter, The Ibis and, in that newsletter, they did name all the new members who had joined in the previous month. In the new month, there’s no mention of an honorary membership being offered to Mr Albanese. There’s nothing in the social committee comments of the time. I couldn’t find any emails on the subject. Essentially, there’s no paper trail to suggest, I can say in all those years before the committee, he was a member, there’s not a single round of golf entered against that golf number’.

‘I won’t be taking lectures from those opposite’: Chalmers rejects calls to resign

I’m sensing a bit of a theme here: Liberal backbencher Leon Rebello is next and he asks Jim Chalmers to “admit he’s run out of steam” and calls for him to resign.

He says Chalmers’ “out of control spending” is driving up inflation, interest rates, and accuses the government of tanking the housing market and killing small business.

Chalmers comes back with a quick quip against his counterpart, Tim Wilson:

It should have rung alarm bells for the honourable member when not even a shadow Treasurer would ask that question, Mr Speaker.

Chalmers then defends his budget:

When it comes to the trillion dollars of debt in the budget, let’s be really clear. Two-thirds of the debt in the budget was racked up by Coalition governments.

“Rubbish!” Shouts a Coalition backbencher. Chalmers continues:

So of all of the people that I will be taking lectures from when it comes to responsible economic management, I won’t be taking lectures from those opposite. They are precisely the last place that I would go for advice on managing the budget.

Tim Wilson continues Coalition attack on treasurer

Shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, is up next and has his go attacking Jim Chalmers.

He has a long preamble citing job losses at large and small businesses and asks Anthony Albanese: “How many more Australians will lose their job before the treasurer loses his?”

The prime minister says the Australian economy is, in fact, pretty good compared with other nations.

Annual economic growth is under pressure, but it’s still stronger than every major advanced economy except for the United States. Inflation is lower than what we inherited and global inflation is having an enormous impact.

I’m [told] by those opposite ‘have a bit of honesty’. Here’s a bit of honesty. More than 1.2m jobs have been created on our watch. We still have the lowest average unemployment of any government in the last 50 years.

Crossbencher says EVs being dumped while companies farm carbon credits

Over to the crossbench, where Rebekha Sharkie asks the government why carbon credits are given to companies for EVs at the point of importation to Australia, rather than when they’re sold.

She says this risks companies dumping EVs for financial incentive and leaves them sitting unsold.

Thousands of Chinese-made EVs are sitting unsold around Australia, dumped at our ports and misused water parks. Many will likely never be sold. Yet many have attracted lucrative carbon credits for their maker.

It’s not often we get a question taken on notice in question time, but Pat Conroy, representing Chris Bowen, says broadly that the government’s EV policy has been critical for decarbonisation:

[Our policy] has led to a very strong take-up of electric vehicles in this country, which is critical to de-carbonising our economy.

headline: California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
body:
Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded

Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.

Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

The controlled detonation at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is now scheduled on Wednesday, November 25, 2026 to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced. The Army and our interagency partners have been working around the clock to safeguard all…

The Army did not respond to a Reuters inquiry on Sunday about the precise timing of the detonation. "Additional details on this situation will be forthcoming," the Army said in its X post.

Lead exposure can cause serious health problems, particularly in children, including ​damage to the brain ​and nervous system.

The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship has recommended that cattle farmers near the detonation site move their livestock, feed and equipment indoors or transport them to alternate ​locations. But farmers have told the environmental council that keeping livestock indoors is not a viable option, Johannsen said.

At least 11 people were killed in a strike on a residential building in Ukraine’s Kyiv region, while several Russian regions reported drone attacks overnight, including on oil infrastructure, according to Ukrainian and Russian officials.

Residents of Novoshakhtinsk reported explosions and a large fire overnight.

Drones also attacked southeastern Tatarstan in the morning, the press service of regional head Rustam Minnikhanov said.

Several oil storage facilities near Almetyevsk were damaged, but there were no casualties, regional authorities said.

headline: 1971, again: a quick scan of who is still speaking
body:
How many of us are genuinely concerned about human rights violations in our backyard?

The backyard is where we look last. How many of us are genuinely concerned about human rights violations there, those lasting decades, involving people whose predicament complicates our national narratives?

I have long asked this about the abandoned Pakistanis of 1971, also called stranded, most of them Biharis, who still "live" in ghettos in Bangladesh.

Whataboutism is distasteful, yet every writer's freedom to choose subject, perspective and silences deserves respect. Nobody's scholarship or right to a platform is in question. But why does one part of this history command sustained attention while the fate of Bihari patriots, and of generations devastated after 1971, remains peripheral? Respecting a writer's choices should not require us to accept collective amnesia.

Why do we so rarely hear Pakistan's intellectual and literary circles speak about the human rights of Pakistanis abandoned in Bangladesh, many living in deeply inhumane conditions

Solidarity with the mazloomeen, the oppressed, of Bucha, Gaza or elsewhere is right, and selective morality must be challenged. This is not about competing tragedies, but universal rights must also reach those closer to home.

Solidarity with the mazloomeen, the oppressed, of Bucha, Gaza or elsewhere is right, and selective morality must be challenged. This is not about competing tragedies, but universal rights must also reach those closer to home.

In the first week of November 2026, I conducted a rapid online archive scan of opinion articles published in The Express Tribune between 1 October 2025 and 31 October 2026. It was a quick scan, not a systematic audit. Using the keywords 1971, Bangladesh, East Pakistan, Fall of Dhaka, stranded Pakistanis, Biharis, Urdu-speaking and Geneva Camp, in headlines or article text, the search yielded 21 op-eds by eight contributors (six men and two women, including myself). They address Bangladesh's political transition, diplomacy, trade, historical grievances and the legacy of 1971.

The limits should be stated plainly. The scan covers a single newspaper, so it is indicative, not representative of Pakistan's wider discourse. My keywords include Bihari-specific terms, and eleven of the 21 pieces are mine, so the count is shaped by my own writing. A keyword search can also miss articles that take up the Bihari question in other words. Readers should weigh the findings accordingly.

The male contributors accounted for nine pieces: Air Vice Marshal (retd) Shahzad Chaudhry (1), Maj Gen(retd) Inam ul Haq(1), Brig (retd) Dr Raashid Wali Janjua (1), Imtiaz Gul (3), Syed Mohammad Ali (1) and Dr Moonis Ahmar (2).

Dr Ahmar has spoken and written about the Bihari question elsewhere, though his articles here during these 13 months focused on other aspects of Bangladesh.

I list these names as data, not as criticism of anyone's choices. Among these articles, I found no headline or central focus addressing the suffering, sacrifices and slaughter of the Biharis, nor their repatriation and right to redistributive justice, by which I mean the state-led reallocation of wealth, resources, property and opportunity to those long denied them. I apologise in advance if my scan missed an empathetic reference by any of them or another contributor.

The sole exception was the other woman writer, Shazia Tasneem Farooqi, whose column "Iqbal Rabbani's Blood-Stained Shirt" (16 December 2025) moved me deeply. By bringing her family's loss into the public narrative, she humanised a history too often reduced to abstractions. Over the same period, The Express Tribune graciously gave me space for eleven opinion pieces examining the Bihari question, the erasure of 1971, Bangladesh's political developments, and our broader obligations of historical and humanitarian empathy. Nine by the men, one by Farooqi and eleven by me make the 21. A twelfth piece of mine, "America at 250: Love, Doubt, and the Debts We Haven't Paid", explored unpaid historical debts in a wider context and also addressed 1971 and the stranded Biharis. I have kept it outside the count of 21.

Political transition, the military history of 1971 and diplomatic rapprochement between Islamabad and Dhaka are important subjects in their own right. But no discussion of Bangladesh is complete without 1971, and no account of 1971 is complete without the devastation it brought to my community. Where, within these conversations, are the people who remain stranded?

My separate independent research on television, "Do Pakistani Television Channels' Current Affairs Talk About the Abandoned Pakistanis of 1971? A Rapid Mapping of Broadcast Journalism (2020 to 16 December 2025)", is available on my websites. It found sustained, agenda-setting engagement difficult to identify across the channels examined. Where the issue did appear, it was a fleeting reference, charity appeal or incidental mention rather than structured inquiry. The periods and methods differ, but the question is the same: what place does this issue hold in our public discourse? Silence in the media matters because it leaves real lives unresolved.

Legal recognition has not ended the problem. Bangladesh's 2008 High Court ruling on citizenship did not reach everyone in the so-called camps, and even those recognised remain unequal in practice, many still living in what are, in reality, ghettos.

The Bihari question is about more than repatriation, citizenship or bilateral relations. It concerns historical responsibility, human dignity and generations left on the margins of political priorities. That responsibility belongs to writers and broadcasters, and also to the state. These people need recognition, rights, security and a durable political solution, not periodic reminders that they exist.

Do we defend human rights as a principle, or only for comfortable stories? Fifty-five years on, generations have been born in those ghettos, and Pakistan rarely says their names. If we can revisit 1971, we can ask what became of those left behind.

Please look again, human rights community, academics, historians, journalists, civil society, think tanks and strategic experts. Pakistan must also counter anti-state literature on 1971 built on unverified or disputed accusations, through dedicated desks and think tanks that respond with documented, evidence-based scholarship.

A stable state can afford introspection. Those who stood with Pakistan's unity deserve its care. Begin with a parliamentary hearing and a clear Foreign Office position.

Stability is measured by the dignity we give our own.

headline: Like SpaceX, Anthropic ran an unusual IPO process, chafing some bankers
body:
Bankers criticised SpaceX's tight control over its IPO process, which limited advisers' access to information.

For the second time this year, Wall Street bankers and lawyers took home a massive paycheck from a record-setting initial public offering. And for the second time this year, some of them came out of it complaining in ​private about how the process was riddled with complications and unlike any they had worked on before.

With SpaceX’s IPO in June, in which banks earned half a billion dollars in fees, bankers chafed over how tightly the Elon Musk-led company ‌controlled the months-long process and kept financial and other information private, making it hard for advisers to do their jobs.

As Anthropic’s ANT.O IPO, dubbed internally “Project Lantern”, eclipsed SpaceX on Thursday and bankers took home more than half a billion dollars in fees, several people close to the process listed a litany of problems that had plagued the offering process: a compressed timeline, marred by last-minute changes and delays in sharing financial projections; rushed document approvals; and highly unusual restrictions on bankers and concern about leaks — especially after Reuters reported many details from a draft IPO filing weeks before it was made public.

Bankers criticised SpaceX's tight control over its IPO process, which limited advisers' access to information.

For the second time this year, Wall Street bankers and lawyers took home a massive paycheck from a record-setting initial public offering. And for the second time this year, some of them came out of it complaining in ​private about how the process was riddled with complications and unlike any they had worked on before.

With SpaceX’s IPO in June, in which banks earned half a billion dollars in fees, bankers chafed over how tightly the Elon Musk-led company ‌controlled the months-long process and kept financial and other information private, making it hard for advisers to do their jobs.

As Anthropic’s ANT.O IPO, dubbed internally “Project Lantern”, eclipsed SpaceX on Thursday and bankers took home more than half a billion dollars in fees, several people close to the process listed a litany of problems that had plagued the offering process: a compressed timeline, marred by last-minute changes and delays in sharing financial projections; rushed document approvals; and highly unusual restrictions on bankers and concern about leaks — especially after Reuters reported many details from a draft IPO filing weeks before it was made public.

Anthropic, for example, instructed some of its 22 IPO underwriters to limit the number of bankers working ​on the deal to four, asking the firms to make sure they were senior staff, several people familiar with the matter said. One of the people said the restriction likely came out of fear that information would leak, and that the banks found a way ​to work around it anyway.

Underlying these complaints is a new power dynamic between technology companies and Wall Street. Companies such as SpaceX, Anthropic — and potentially also OpenAI in the future — have come to wield enormous power as ⁠the transformative potential of artificial intelligence creates a frenzied demand for their shares, and they are wielding it to do things their way. That is upsetting some bankers. But banks and investors appear to have little choice but to play along.

“These companies certainly did have some market power to ​tell underwriters that it’s not going to be business as usual,” said Jay Ritter, a University of Florida professor emeritus who researches IPOs. “But the big Wall Street firms, I suspect, are still going to be doing things as business as usual for all but maybe OpenAI (after these two deals).”

Read More: EU proposes tax on Big Tech to boost budget

Ritter added ​that both SpaceX and Anthropic had negotiated to pay underwriters nothing on the additional shares sold through the greenshoe option. “I don't think most companies are going to be able to demand zero spread on overallotment shares,” he said.

Anthropic, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, the two lead underwriters on the two IPOs, declined to comment.

SpaceX and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment.

Both SpaceX and Anthropic debuted successfully, raising record amounts of money, and their shares rallied initially. A key part of the underwriters’ job is to market the securities. Thanks to the demand for AI, that was an easy sell — both companies had order books oversubscribed many times over.

After an initial burst ​in shares, the trajectories of the two big AI firms diverged. SpaceX climbed to a post-listing peak of $201.80 on June 16 before retreating below its $135 IPO price for the first time in mid-July. Anthropic’s shares closed down 8.5% on Friday after a 17% first-day pop, as a dramatic unraveling ​of the AI trade showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector.

In the case of SpaceX’s IPO, the people close to the process said Musk’s team dictated terms at every stage. Musk's team told the largest and most powerful US banks — including Goldman Sachs ‌and Morgan Stanley — how ⁠to market SpaceX's stock and to whom. It told some banks the specific order sizes they needed to “fill” — in some cases a few billion dollars — and gave them instructions on what types of investors to bring. Banks signed on to underwrite the IPO without being told what they would be paid, the people said.

The underlying current running through Anthropic’s IPO process was what several of the people who spoke to Reuters interpreted as a sense of extreme caution.

Anthropic asked some senior officers at banks working on its IPO to sign legal documents restricting core members of the transaction team from working with rival companies, including OpenAI, Cursor, DeepSeek and Hugging Face, for six months after it went public, according to the people.

Banks routinely manage conflicts and protect client confidentiality. But bankers and lawyers said it is rare for an IPO to impose exclusivity this broad, particularly on individual bankers.

In previous head-to-head IPOs ​such as those of ridesharing rivals Uber (UBER.N), opens new tab and Lyft (LYFT.O), opens new tab, or real ​estate companies Trulia and Zillow (ZG.O), opens new tab, banks could simply pick a side, ⁠in part because the deals were smaller and required fewer banks.

Anthropic, by contrast, needed a broad syndicate to raise the enormous amount of capital it was seeking. That, some of the people said, explained why Anthropic sought to bind individual bankers with these restrictions.

One banker who declined to sign on to the agreement said it was a challenge to find people who could promise not to actively cover or engage with Anthropic’s peers, especially as ​several of those companies pursue their own initial or secondary offerings.

Some of the restrictions were meant to control leaks of information.

Nearly four weeks before Anthropic’s filing with the Securities and Exchange ​Commission, called Form S-1, was made public, ⁠Reuters reported on it, revealing details of the company’s financials, risk factors, dealings with other tech companies and other information.

Anthropic also used a product called NetRoadshow to share information, instead of regular PDFs, with most of the banks underwriting the deal.

NetRoadshow logs access details, including information such as who has seen the document and looked at which page. Documents on NetRoadshow also had individual bankers’ names as watermarks.

Leaks continued to surface in the press, but using NetRoadshow complicated bankers' work, including because the platform would not let them save copies of documents, one of the people said.

Anthropic planned to file an updated securities filing, called an ⁠S-1A, with the SEC ​with the price range and to launch the marketing on November 10. To do so, it needed to send a draft to all the banks in its syndicate for ​them to sign off on it.

The night before it was to happen, a law firm on the deal sent a PDF to the banks about the sale of shares in Canada. But soon it followed with another email asking them to disregard it, saying it “contains incorrect price range and share information,” according to the email, which was seen by Reuters.

The correct S-1A ​was then sent via the NetRoadshow platform around 2 a.m. New York time. Banks were told they had several hours to sign off on it before it was filed with the SEC.

headline: Indonesia says 24 killed in factory blaze as rescuers search for dozens missing
body:
Presidential adviser says implementation of safety protocols being assessed, factory's chief executive to be summoned

Indonesia confirmed on Monday the deaths of 24 people in a fire that tore through a factory at the weekend, as rescuers braved unstable structures in the burned wreckage in the search for about 30 people still missing.

Authorities were still investigating the cause of the fire, which broke out on Saturday evening in one building of the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia confectionery factory in Cikande in Banten province, about an hour's drive from the capital Jakarta.

Said Iqbal, a presidential adviser on labour issues, told reporters 24 people had died, adding implementation of safety protocols was being assessed and that he would summon the factory's chief executive. Preliminary reports indicated the fire may have been caused by an air-conditioner short circuit, Said added.

The factory is owned by United Family Food, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The firm employs about 5,000 people overall and is a major supplier of consumer goods to the domestic market, with four overseas offices. Its products include Milkita, a popular confectionery brand, and Lemonilo, an instant noodle variety, according to its website.

The factory's CEO Steven Erwin Wijaya has said about 300 people were present at the factory complex for Saturday's shift.

headline: Scientist Two and the new knowledge frontier
body:
Pakistan's next AI policy challenge may be how to govern a research system in which machines can generate hypotheses, run experiments, write code, draft papers and even review one another.

A September 2026 Google Cloud AI Research preprint, ScientistTwo, offers a glimpse of that future. Given a human-defined scientific problem, its multi-agent system identifies weaknesses in existing work, proposes new ideas, runs experiments, performs ablation studies, drafts a paper and sends it through simulated peer review and rebuttal. The authors report that it improved 86 of 107 machine-learning research problems, an 80.4% success rate, with an average 25.2% gain over human state-of-the-art baselines.

The full cycle reportedly took about two to three days and cost roughly $3,800 per task. Those figures require caution. This is a preprint; its benchmarks are predominantly computational AI problems, and much of its evaluation relies on AI reviewers. The authors themselves concede that the system does not yet consistently produce the kind of paradigm-changing work associated with top conference spotlight or oral papers.

Yet the direction is difficult to ignore: the cost of producing plausible scientific work may fall much faster than the cost of verifying it.

A September 2026 Google Cloud AI Research preprint, ScientistTwo, offers a glimpse of that future. The full cycle reportedly took about two to three days and cost roughly $3,800 per task. Those figures require caution. This is a preprint; its benchmarks are predominantly computational AI problems, and much of its evaluation relies on AI reviewers. The authors themselves concede that the system does not yet consistently produce the kind of paradigm-changing work associated with top conference spotlight or oral papers.

Yet the direction is difficult to ignore: the cost of producing plausible scientific work may fall much faster than the cost of verifying it.

WIPO's Global Innovation Index 2026 ranks Pakistan 95th overall, but reveals a striking imbalance: 121st in innovation inputs and 72nd in outputs. WIPO again identifies Pakistan as an innovation "overperformer", producing comparatively stronger outputs from constrained inputs. Its strengths include ICT-services exports, ranked 15th globally, and scientific production, ranked 49th. Meanwhile, Pakistan's Economic Survey reports ICT export remittances of $3.38 billion during July-March FY2026, up 19.7% year-on-year.

This is the kind of economy that could benefit disproportionately from autonomous research. Pakistan cannot quickly reproduce the laboratories, endowments or researcher density of richer economies. But it may be able to compress parts of the discovery cycle through shared compute, scientific agents and better access to data.

The danger is equally obvious. If universities continue rewarding publication counts while machines make papers cheaper to produce, Pakistan could automate the wrong thing.

Pakistan should establish a National Verified Research Grid that shares infrastructure connecting the national AI compute grid already envisaged under the National AI Policy with universities, scientific databases, public datasets, software and autonomous research agents. The existing policy already proposes a national network of high-performance computing centers, GPUs and specialised AI hardware. The next step should be to connect that compute to national problems rather than simply "AI projects".

Ministries could publish challenge statements around important national issues, for instance, crop productivity, flood forecasting, disease surveillance, water losses, industrial energy efficiency, logistics and tax compliance. Universities and research teams would compete for compute based on measurable outcomes.

Albeit, the Grid needs an unusual second layer, a National Research Ledger.

Every publicly funded AI-assisted study should carry a machine-readable "research passport": which model generated which hypothesis, which datasets were used, what code was executed, which results were machine-produced, what was independently reproduced and which human investigator accepted responsibility for the final claim.

This is not technological fantasy. ScientistTwo itself employs integrity checks for reproducibility, rule violations, hallucinated references and whether the manuscript accurately represents the underlying code. Pakistan could convert that technical principle into institutional governance.

An AI-generated finding may be published as exploratory research. But it should not automatically qualify for academic promotion, public procurement, clinical guidance, regulation or major government policy until an independent replication or audit crosses a defined verification threshold. Medicine, infrastructure, defence and public finance should face higher thresholds than low-risk computational research.

Universities would also need to rethink incentives. HEC has already adopted a framework that moves away from blanket prohibition of generative AI towards responsible use and AI literacy. The next step is separating authorship from accountability.

A PhD should eventually be judged less by whether three papers were produced and more by whether the researcher formulated an important problem, developed defensible theory, interrogated causality, verified the evidence and can explain why a result deserves to be believed.

Government could push this further by replacing part of publication-based research funding with a Verified National Problems programme. Universities would earn competitive funding when independently reproduced research improves an agreed public metric.

There is an economic opportunity here too. Pakistan's next step beyond software freelancing could be research-as-a-service.

Science traditionally moves from human curiosity to hypothesis, experiment, criticism and accepted knowledge. Autonomous systems can now occupy several links in that chain. The scarce resource may therefore migrate from producing research to judging it.

Pakistan should neither ban the machine scientist nor worship it. It should build institutions around a harder principle that AI may generate knowledge claims, but accountable institutions must certify that knowledge.

headline: Naqvi, Shujaat discuss creation of new provinces amid growing political debate
body:
Shujaat says creation of new provinces directly linked to public convenience, better governance

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Monday visited the Lahore residence of Pakistan Muslim League-Quaid (PML-Q) chief Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain and met with him to discuss the country's overall situation and the government's measures to maintain law and order.

The two also discussed the devolution of powers to the grassroots level, including the establishment of new provinces.

Shujaat said the creation of new provinces was directly linked to public convenience, better governance, administrative efficiency and the country's future. He said strengthening and empowering administrative units could also be an effective way forward.

"Ordinary citizens are Pakistan's biggest stakeholders," he said, adding that the country would not forgive its leaders if they failed to take the right steps today.

Naqvi said it was imperative to take all decisions in accordance with the wishes of the people of Pakistan. The interior minister also briefed Shujaat on measures taken to counter terrorism and maintain peace in Balochistan and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa.

Federal Minister for Overseas Pakistanis Chaudhry Salik Hussain and Punjab Industries Minister Chaudhry Shafay Hussain were also present at the meeting.

The Sindh Assembly also passed a resolution on September 4 rejecting attempts to divide the province or alter its geographical boundaries.

Meanwhile, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif has supported the idea of creating as many as 12 provinces, arguing that smaller administrative units could improve governance and service delivery.

The demand for new provinces is longstanding, with calls for separate provincial status in South Punjab, Bahawalpur and Hazara based on arguments concerning administrative convenience, political representation and development disparities. headline: Atalanta grab dramatic draw with Inter in Serie A
body:
Elmas, De Ketelaere (2) and Kessie cancel out Esposito's treble in a 4-4 stalemate

Atalanta rescued an extraordinary late 4-4 draw against Inter Milan on Sunday as the champions fell three points off the Serie A title pace despite Francesco Pio Esposito's hat-trick, while AC Milan and Juventus claimed big wins.

The conflict in Myanmar has continued since the military seized power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in February 2021, triggering widespread protests, a military crackdown and an armed resistance movement.

Rejecting criticism of its handling of the conflict, Myanmar said it had continued to cooperate with ASEAN's suggestions and recommendations while safeguarding its national interests and sovereignty.

The Ministry asserted that "there are no political prisoners" in the country, maintaining that individuals were serving sentences under existing laws.

The statement also defended the government's security operations, saying it had undertaken only measures necessary to safeguard the country's sovereignty and protect its people, while exercising "utmost restraint" and employing minimum force in accordance with domestic laws and applicable Rules of Engagement.

The Ministry criticised ASEAN for what it described as inconsistent adherence to the principles of sovereignty, equality, non-interference and consensus-based decision-making enshrined in the ASEAN Charter.

Questioning the continued restrictions on its leadership's participation in ASEAN summits, the Ministry said such treatment was discriminatory and inconsistent with the bloc's charter and established practices.

The statement came amid renewed international scrutiny of Myanmar, with the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague having delivered a landmark judgment last week finding the country responsible for committing genocide against the Rohingya during the 2017 military clearance operations in northern Rakhine State.

Netanyahu is pushing for a national unity government, which could see a rotation of the premiership between the two men, a mechanism already tried in Israel.

Such an arrangement could allow Netanyahu to keep his political protection against the corruption charges he faces, as well as continue to oppose the creation of an independent commission of inquiry into the security failures that preceded the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023.

But that prospect runs up against Eisenkot's refusal to serve in a cabinet led by Netanyahu, against whom he centred his campaign.

His ally Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister, also reiterated on Saturday his refusal to join a coalition with "Netanyahu or his bloc, under any circumstances".

On Saturday (November 22), Yashar presented the resumption of talks as "a genuine commitment to forming the broadest possible government", saying that Eisenkot had asked his representatives to explore all options.

But Likud immediately laid down several conditions for its participation in a unity government, a formula backed by Mr. Netanyahu.

Among other things, it demands an end to "all personal attacks and incitement to hatred" targeting Mr. Netanyahu and his government.

It also called for bringing together "all the parties that support the existence of the State of Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people", without the participation of Arab parties.

Mr. Netanyahu and his allies regularly target Arab parties, which secured a record 19 seats in the legislature and are opposed to Mr. Netanyahu remaining in power.

Likud is also demanding agreement on several major policy positions, notably rejecting the creation of a Palestinian state, maintaining Israeli control over territories in Syria, Lebanon and the Gaza Strip.

It is also pushing for a compromise on conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jews, a particularly sensitive issue in Israel.

On Friday (November 20), Mr. Eisenkot warned that he would not allow the talks to drag on, saying he was ready to submit to parliament an "emergency national government".

Although he did not spell out how, his statements suggest a two-stage plan: the swift formation of a minority government based on the core opposition parties, and then broadening it.
